name: Classic-Style Test 1
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City planner: Some residents argue that Harlow’s downtown parking garage should be demolished because it is rarely more than half full. But the garage’s low usage reflects its high hourly rates, which the council set before the new transit line reduced downtown traffic. Lowering those rates would probably fill the garage. So the garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the city planner’s argument?
choices: The downtown garage should not be demolished at least until lower hourly rates have been tried there.
The garage is rarely more than half full mainly because the council set its hourly rates too high.
Lowering the garage’s hourly rates would probably bring in enough additional drivers to fill the garage.
The council set the garage’s current rates before the new transit line reduced the amount of downtown traffic.
Residents who want the garage demolished have misjudged how heavily the garage is actually being used by drivers.
questions.explanation: The planner’s point, signaled by “So,” is that the garage should be kept until lower rates are tried, which (A) restates. (C) is the tempting choice, but the prediction about lower rates is offered as a reason for keeping the garage; (B) is likewise a supporting premise. (E) misreads the planner, who accepts that usage is low and disputes only its cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Low usage is caused by high rates, set before the transit line cut traffic; lowering the rates would probably fill the garage.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. This is a rebuttal: the residents say tear it down because it's half empty. The planner says the emptiness comes from the prices, cheaper prices would fill it, so keep it until we try that. The word "So" flags the conclusion. Think of a restaurant owner saying: "The new dish isn't selling because it's overpriced, a lower price would sell it, so don't pull it off the menu yet." The point is "don't pull it yet," not the pricing story.

choices.note: CORRECT. "Kept, at least until lower rates have been tried" means the same thing as "not demolished at least until lower rates have been tried." It's what the "So" introduces and what every other sentence is there to support.
This is a premise. The planner uses the high-rates explanation to undercut the residents' reason. It supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.

Tempting. It's the planner's boldest claim, so it feels like the point. But ask why the planner says it: to show the garage is worth keeping. A prediction offered as a reason is a premise. The conclusion is the claim the others are trying to prove, not the most interesting one.
Background detail. It explains why the rates are now too high. It sits at the bottom of the support structure.
The planner never says the residents misjudged usage. The planner accepts that the garage is rarely more than half full and only disputes what that fact means. Wrong claim attributed to the speaker.

questions.stimulus:
Ana: The old mill on Fenwick Creek should be restored and opened as a museum. It is the town’s last link to the industry on which the town was founded, and visitors would see how our community grew.

Ben: The mill is certainly historically important. But restoring it would cost far more than the town could ever raise. The town should instead put up a plaque and a small exhibit at the library, which would preserve the mill’s story cheaply.
questions.stem: Ana and Ben disagree over whether
choices: the mill is the town’s last remaining link to the industry on which the town was founded
restoring the mill would cost more money than the town could realistically ever raise
the town should restore the mill and then open it to the public as a museum
the history associated with the mill is worth preserving for future residents in some form
visitors would learn more from a museum in the mill than from an exhibit at the library
questions.explanation: Ana says the mill should be restored as a museum; Ben says restoration costs too much and the town should do something cheaper instead, so they disagree over (C). (D) is the trap: both value the mill’s history, so they agree on it. (A) is Ana’s claim alone, (B) is Ben’s alone, and neither speaker compares what visitors would learn, as (E) requires.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ana: Restore the mill as a museum; it's the town's last link to its founding industry.; Ben: It's historically important, but restoring it costs far too much; put up a plaque and a library exhibit instead.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ana says: restore it, make it a museum. Ben says: too expensive, do this cheaper thing instead. That "instead" is Ben's no. Notice what they share: both think the mill's story matters. Ben even calls it "certainly historically important." So history is common ground, and the fight is over the museum.

choices.note: Ana's claim only. Ben never says whether the mill is the town's last link to its founding industry; he says only that it is historically important. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Ben's claim only. Ana never addresses cost, so we can't say she rejects it.
CORRECT. Ana says the mill should be restored and opened as a museum. Ben says restoration costs more than the town could raise and the town should "instead" do a plaque and exhibit. Yes versus no.

Tempting, because the dialogue is all about history. But this is what they agree on: Ana wants the history shown, and Ben wants to "preserve the mill's story." Agreement is not a point of disagreement.
Neither speaker compares what visitors would learn from a museum versus an exhibit. Ana mentions visitors, but she doesn't rank the two options. Unsupported for both.

questions.stimulus: The Ridgeway Observatory recently replaced its aging telescope with a new one whose much larger mirror gathers far more light, making faint galaxies considerably easier to detect. Yet in its first year of use, the new telescope detected fewer faint galaxies in total than the old telescope had detected in its final year, even though astronomers aimed both instruments at the same regions of the sky.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Telescopes with larger mirrors cost considerably more to build and maintain than telescopes with smaller mirrors do.
In its first year, the new telescope was often shut down for calibration and so observed far fewer hours.
Faint galaxies are considerably harder for any telescope to detect than bright galaxies at a comparable distance are.
The observatory’s astronomers had expected the new telescope to detect many more faint galaxies than the old one detected.
The old telescope had been in continuous use at the observatory for several decades before it was finally replaced.
questions.explanation: A better instrument can still produce a smaller total if it is used much less, and (B) says the new telescope spent far less time observing, which resolves the puzzle. (D) merely restates the expectation that makes the result surprising, and (C) is true of both telescopes alike, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new telescope gathers far more light and makes faint galaxies easier to detect, but in its first year it detected fewer faint galaxies in total than the old one did in its last year.

breakdown.analysis: How can a better tool produce a smaller total? Totals depend on two things: how good the tool is and how much it gets used. The stimulus rules out "it looked at different sky," so look for something that made the new telescope get used less. It's like buying a faster car and still logging fewer miles this year because it sat in the shop for months. Prephrase: the new telescope wasn't observing as much.

choices.note: Cost has nothing to do with how many galaxies it detects once it's built. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. Fewer hours of observing means fewer chances to detect anything. Even a far better telescope can rack up a smaller total if it's shut down for calibration much of the year. Both facts in the paradox can now be true.
True of both telescopes equally. A fact that applies to both sides can't explain a difference between them. In a paradox about a comparison, you need a factor that differs between the two things.
This just restates why the result is surprising. Expectations don't explain why the expectations weren't met.
So the old telescope was old. That makes it even stranger that it beat the new one. Doesn't resolve anything.

questions.stimulus: In a recent survey of dog owners, those who walk their dogs on retractable leashes reported far more incidents of their dogs lunging at passersby than did those who use fixed-length leashes. The two groups of owners walked their dogs for about the same amount of time each day. Evidently, the extra slack that retractable leashes provide encourages dogs to lunge.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on reports from dog owners rather than on observations made by professional trainers or other neutral experts
presumes, without providing justification, that any dog that lunges at passersby must have been poorly trained by its owner
takes for granted that every dog walked on a retractable leash will at some point lunge at passersby
overlooks the possibility that owners of dogs prone to lunging are more likely to choose retractable leashes
treats the fact that lunging at passersby is undesirable as evidence that such lunging is common among dogs
questions.explanation: The argument infers that the leash causes the lunging from a mere correlation, ignoring that the dogs themselves may differ: owners of lunge-prone dogs might favor retractable leashes, which is (D). (A) is tempting because self-reports can be unreliable, but nothing turns on owners being worse judges than trainers of whether their dogs lunge. (C) attributes a claim about every dog that the argument never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extra slack of retractable leashes encourages dogs to lunge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Owners using retractable leashes reported far more lunging incidents than owners using fixed-length leashes; both groups walked their dogs about equally long.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the two go together? Correlation isn't causation. The argument even rules out one rival (more walking time), but not the biggest one: the dogs may be different to begin with. Maybe owners of wild, pully dogs pick retractable leashes because those dogs hate short leads. It's like saying hospitals make people sick because people in hospitals are sicker than people outside. Prephrase: the argument ignores that the dogs on retractable leashes may already be more lunge-prone.

choices.note: Tempting, because self-reports can be shaky. But owners are perfectly able to notice their dog lunging, and nothing in the argument depends on owners being worse judges than trainers. This names a source problem the argument doesn't really have.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our customers say our coffee is the best in town, so it must be better than any coffee a professional taster has rated.

choices.note: Training never comes up. The argument blames the leash, not poor training, so this describes an assumption the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of flaw: That dog jumped on a guest, so its owner obviously never trained it.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument talks about more incidents in one group, not that every retractable-leash dog lunges. It doesn't need or assume an "every" claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Retractable leashes encourage lunging, so my neighbor's dog, which is on one, must lunge at people.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the alternative explanation: the dogs differ before the leash ever enters the picture. If lunge-prone dogs end up on retractable leashes, leash type would correlate with lunging even if slack had zero effect.
The argument never argues from lunging being undesirable, and it's not trying to prove lunging is common. It's a causal claim about leashes. Describes a different flaw entirely.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Littering is terrible, so it must be happening all over this park.

questions.stimulus: Last spring the Alder Street Bistro began printing calorie counts beside each item on its menu. Since then, sales of the bistro’s two highest-calorie desserts have fallen by nearly a third, while sales of its fruit plates have risen by about the same number of orders. The bistro’s owner concludes that the calorie counts led many diners to choose lighter desserts.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner’s argument?
choices: Several regular diners have told the owner that they appreciate being able to see calorie counts on the menu.
Over the same period, dessert sales at nearby restaurants that do not print calorie counts showed no comparable shift.
The bistro’s two highest-calorie desserts are also the most expensive desserts that the bistro offers on its menu.
Many of the bistro’s diners say that they rarely read the menu closely before deciding what to order.
Last spring the bistro also hired a new pastry chef, who redesigned the fruit plates and their presentation.
questions.explanation: The owner attributes a sales shift to the calorie counts, so the argument is helped by evidence that the shift did not happen where there were no calorie counts, as (B) shows; that makes a general change in tastes a less likely cause. (A) is tempting but shows only that diners like the counts, not that the counts changed what they ordered. (E) offers a rival explanation and (D) suggests diners ignored the counts, so both weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The calorie counts led many diners to choose lighter desserts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the menu started showing calorie counts, sales of the two highest-calorie desserts fell almost a third and fruit plate sales rose.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causal argument. Calorie counts went up, then heavy dessert sales went down, so the counts did it. But did anything else change? A citywide diet trend or the season could do the same thing. To strengthen, rule out those rivals. The cleanest way is a control group: places without calorie counts that didn't see the shift. It's like testing a new fertilizer: your tomatoes grew bigger, but did your neighbor's unfertilized tomatoes grow bigger too?

choices.note: Tempting, but liking the counts isn't the same as changing what you order. A diner can appreciate the information and still order the chocolate cake. Doesn't connect counts to choices.

CORRECT. This is the control group. Nearby restaurants without calorie counts saw no similar shift, so a general change in tastes or the weather is less likely to be the cause. That leaves the calorie counts looking more like the reason.
If anything this hurts. If the heavy desserts are also the priciest, maybe people cut back because of price. It opens a rival cause rather than supporting the calorie explanation.
This weakens. If diners barely read the menu, it's hard for numbers printed on the menu to be driving their choices.

Weakens. A new pastry chef who redesigned the fruit plates is a rival explanation for why fruit plates got more popular, at exactly the same time. An answer that adds a second change during the same period almost always hurts a before-and-after argument.

questions.stimulus: Principal: This year our school stopped assigning weekend homework, chiefly in order to reduce student stress. Yet students’ average score on the annual stress survey, which every student completes each spring, is no lower this year than it was last year. So, whatever its other merits, eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the principal’s argument?
choices: Students who no longer have weekend homework now spend more of their weekend time on extracurricular activities.
Reducing the amount of homework is the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.
Students’ average score on the stress survey was higher this year than it was in the previous year.
Most students had regularly been completing all of their weekend homework before the new policy took effect.
No other change this year raised students’ stress enough to offset a reduction due to the policy.
questions.explanation: Unchanged survey scores show the policy failed only if nothing else pushed stress up at the same time; if some other change raised stress by as much as the policy lowered it, the flat scores would hide a real effect. That is (E). (B) is tempting but goes much further than needed, and (C) is not required, since unchanged scores are enough for the argument. Negating (D) actually helps the principal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The policy started this year; average stress survey scores are no lower than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Do flat scores really mean the policy did nothing? Not if two forces cancel out: the policy lowers stress while something else raises it. Picture a diet that works, but you also stopped exercising, and the scale doesn't move. The diet still worked. We need an answer that says nothing else was pushing stress up enough to mask the drop. Use the negation test: if negating a choice wrecks the argument, it's required.

choices.note: Negate it and nothing happens. Whether students moved to extracurriculars or not, the argument is about the stress scores. Irrelevant.
choices.negation: Students who no longer have weekend homework do not spend more of their weekend time on extracurricular activities.

choices.note: Too strong. The principal only claims this policy didn't work, not anything about which method is best. Negate it (homework cuts aren't the best method) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Reducing the amount of homework is not the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.

choices.note: Not required. "No lower" already does the job. Negated, scores weren't higher (say, exactly the same), and the argument works just fine.
choices.negation: Students' average score on the stress survey was not higher this year than it was in the previous year.

choices.note: Tempting, since if kids weren't doing the homework anyway, cutting it couldn't help. But that would actually support the principal's conclusion. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument; it gives another reason the policy might not have worked.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students had regularly been completing all of their weekend homework before the new policy took effect.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, some other change did raise stress enough to offset a real reduction. Then flat scores tell you nothing about the policy, and the conclusion falls apart. Negation destroys the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Some other change this year raised students' stress enough to offset a reduction due to the policy.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director: Last year, customers who bought our Lumo vacuum with the extended warranty brought it in for repairs far less often than customers who bought it without the warranty. The warranty includes a free yearly tune-up that other customers do not receive. So the tune-up must be reducing the number of breakdowns these vacuums suffer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director’s argument?
choices: During each yearly tune-up, technicians fix any malfunction they find, and such fixes are not recorded as repairs.
Customers who did not buy the extended warranty must pay the full cost of any repair their vacuum needs.
Lumo vacuums break down less often, on average, than most competing vacuums sold in the same price range.
Most customers who bought the extended warranty brought their vacuums in for the free yearly tune-up last year.
The extended warranty costs about one-fifth as much as the vacuum itself when the two are bought together.
questions.explanation: The director treats fewer recorded repair visits as evidence of fewer breakdowns. (A) shows the comparison is skewed: warranty holders’ malfunctions are often fixed during tune-ups and never counted as repairs, so their lower repair count need not mean fewer breakdowns. (D) strengthens the argument by confirming that warranty holders actually got the tune-ups, and (B), if anything, strengthens it too: customers who must pay for repairs would tend to bring vacuums in less often, yet they still had more repair visits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The free yearly tune-up must be reducing breakdowns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Warranty customers brought their vacuums in for repairs less often than non-warranty customers; only warranty customers get the yearly tune-up.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of repair visits really the same as the number of breakdowns? Notice the switch: the evidence is about repair visits, but the conclusion is about breakdowns. If breakdowns get fixed some other way, repair visits can drop even when breakdowns don't. It's like saying a gym's members get sick less because they file fewer sick-day forms, when the gym's clinic quietly treats them on site. We need an answer that says warranty holders' breakdowns are being handled without counting as repair visits.

choices.note: CORRECT. Malfunctions get fixed during the tune-up and aren't recorded as repairs. So warranty holders could break down just as often; their breakdowns just show up as tune-ups. The lower repair count no longer shows fewer breakdowns.

Tempting, because it points to a difference between the groups. But it pushes the wrong way: non-warranty customers have to pay, which should make them come in less, yet they still came in more. That makes their higher repair rate look like real breakdowns.
Comparing Lumo to competitors doesn't touch the comparison between warranty and non-warranty Lumo owners. Irrelevant.
This strengthens. It confirms warranty customers actually got the tune-ups, which the argument needs.

Price of the warranty is irrelevant to whether the tune-up reduces breakdowns. You might wonder if pricey warranties attract careful owners, but this choice doesn't say that, and you can't pick an answer on a possibility.

questions.stimulus: Every project paid for from the city’s parks budget must first be approved by the neighborhood advisory board, and the board approves only projects that are open to the public. The proposed rooftop garden on City Hall would be reachable only through a secured employee entrance. Thus, the rooftop garden cannot be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The advisory board has approved every project it has reviewed that would be open to the public.
Some projects that have been paid for from the parks budget are not open to members of the public.
No facility that is reachable only through a secured employee entrance is open to the public.
The rooftop garden would benefit city employees considerably more than it would benefit the city’s other residents.
If a proposed project would be open to the public, it can be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.explanation: The chain is: parks funding requires board approval, and board approval requires being open to the public. The missing link connects “reachable only through a secured employee entrance” to “not open to the public,” and (C) supplies it, so the garden cannot get approval and therefore cannot get funding. (A) and (E) reverse the conditionals and say what is enough for approval or funding, which cannot show that the garden is barred. (B) conflicts with the stated rules.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rooftop garden cannot be paid for from the parks budget.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Parks funding → board approval; board approval → open to the public; the garden is reachable only through a secured employee entrance.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Parks-funded → board-approved → open to public. Contrapositive: not open to public → not board-approved → not parks-funded. To get the conclusion, we need the garden to be not open to the public. The premise only says it's reachable only through a secured employee entrance. Missing link: secured-employee-entrance-only → not open to public. Plug that in and the chain runs all the way to "can't be paid for from parks."

choices.note: This reverses the second rule. It says open to public → approved, which is the sufficient direction for getting approval. We need something that blocks approval, not something that grants it.
This contradicts the rules: every parks project needs approval and approval needs public access, so no parks project can be closed to the public. And it doesn't link the garden to anything.
CORRECT. Secured-employee-entrance-only → not open to public. The garden is secured-entrance-only, so not open, so not approved, so not parks-funded. The conclusion follows with certainty.
Who benefits is irrelevant to the conditional rules. Doesn't link the garden to public access.
Reversed. Open to public → can be funded. That tells you what's enough to qualify, not what disqualifies. Doesn't get you to "cannot."

questions.stimulus: At the Linden animal shelter, cats housed in the shelter’s quiet rooms have long been adopted more quickly than cats housed in the noisy main kennel area. Last fall, hoping to speed adoptions, the shelter soundproofed another room and moved half of its main-area cats into it. Yet the cats that were moved were not adopted any more quickly than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why moving the cats did not shorten their adoption times?
choices: Cats in the main kennel area are frequently exposed to the noise of dogs barking in a nearby wing.
Most people who adopt cats from the Linden shelter visit on weekends, when the shelter is at its busiest.
The newly soundproofed room is larger and brighter than any of the other quiet rooms at the shelter.
Some cats housed in the main kennel area have been adopted within a day of arriving at the shelter.
Until last fall, the shelter placed only its calmest and most sociable cats in the quiet rooms.
questions.explanation: If the shelter had been putting its calmest, most sociable cats in the quiet rooms, those cats’ faster adoptions reflected their temperaments rather than the quiet, so giving other cats a quiet room would not be expected to help. That is (E). (A) is tempting because it explains why the main area might seem unappealing, but it gives no reason why removing the noise failed to help. (C) would, if anything, lead one to expect better results.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cats in the quiet rooms have long been adopted faster than cats in the noisy main area, but cats moved into a newly soundproofed room were adopted no faster than before.

breakdown.analysis: The shelter assumed the quiet caused the faster adoptions. If moving cats into quiet didn't help, maybe quiet was never the cause. Look for something else that made quiet-room cats special. It's like noticing that students in the honors classroom score higher, moving regular students into that room, and seeing no change: the room wasn't what made the honors students score higher. Prephrase: the quiet-room cats were different cats to begin with.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains why the main area is unpleasant. But that makes the puzzle worse: if noise is the problem, removing it should have helped. Doesn't explain the failure.
Weekend visiting applies to all cats equally. It doesn't explain why moved cats got no boost.
A bigger, brighter quiet room should, if anything, help more. This deepens the puzzle instead of solving it.
A few speedy main-area adoptions don't explain why the moved cats saw no improvement. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. The quiet rooms held the calmest, friendliest cats, and those traits are what got them adopted fast. The quiet itself wasn't doing the work. So moving ordinary cats into quiet wouldn't speed things up.

questions.stimulus: The manager of the Summit Wall climbing gym wanted to learn whether members would support ending the gym’s 6 a.m. opening in exchange for keeping the gym open until midnight. For two weeks, front-desk staff asked every member who checked in before 8 a.m. for an opinion, and nearly 90 percent opposed the change. Clearly, most of the gym’s members want the early opening kept.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that members who oppose a change in hours will cancel their memberships if it is made
fails to consider whether keeping the gym open until midnight would substantially raise the gym’s staffing and utility costs
treats the fact that most surveyed members opposed the change as proof that the change would be unprofitable for the gym
infers what most members prefer from the opinions of members who are especially likely to favor the early opening
overlooks the possibility that some members who check in before 8 a.m. would also use the gym late at night
questions.explanation: The only members polled were those who arrive before 8 a.m., the people most likely to value the 6 a.m. opening, so their answers cannot show what most members want; (D) describes this. (E) is tempting because it is about the surveyed group, but early arrivals who might also come late still opposed the change. (B) and (C) shift to cost and profit, which the conclusion never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the gym's members want the early opening kept.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly 90 percent of members asked at check-in before 8 a.m. opposed ending the 6 a.m. opening.

breakdown.analysis: Who did they ask? Only the people who show up before 8 a.m. Of course they want the gym to open at 6. That's like polling people at a breakfast diner about whether the diner should stop serving breakfast. The sample is built to favor one answer, so it can't stand for all members. This is an unrepresentative sample. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the surveyed members were especially likely to want the early hours.

choices.note: The argument never says anyone will cancel. It's about what members prefer, not what they'll do. Describes an assumption the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most members dislike the new music, so if we keep it, most of them will quit.

choices.note: So? Costs might matter to the decision, but the conclusion is only about what members want. Wrong dimension.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Members want longer hours, so we should add them, since nothing else could matter.

choices.note: Profit never comes up. The conclusion is about preference, not money.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most diners we asked disliked the new dish, so it is bound to lose money.

choices.note: CORRECT. Early-morning arrivals are exactly the members who'd lose the most if the 6 a.m. opening ended. Their opinions can't stand in for the whole membership, which may include many night owls who were never asked.

Tempting, since it talks about the surveyed group. But even if some early arrivals would also come late at night, they still told staff they opposed the change. This doesn't expose any gap between the sample and the whole membership.

questions.stimulus: At Wexford Design, an employee’s request to work a flexible schedule should be granted whenever the employee’s duties do not require being present at fixed hours, provided that granting the request would not shift any work onto coworkers and the employee has met every deadline during the past six months. Requests that do not meet these conditions are decided case by case.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Rina’s duties do not require fixed hours, and she has met every deadline this year. So her request for a flexible schedule should be granted, even though coworkers would have to cover her morning calls.
Priya’s work can be done at any hour, and none of her tasks would fall to her team. She has missed no deadline in over a year, so her request should be granted.
Lena’s duties do not require fixed hours, and no work would shift to her coworkers. But she missed a deadline last month, so her request for a flexible schedule should be denied.

Omar’s request would shift no work to his coworkers, and his duties do not require fixed hours. So his request should be granted, since his supervisor considers him one of the department’s best performers.
Tomas has met every deadline for six months, and his flexible schedule would not burden his coworkers. So his request should be granted, even though he must staff the front desk from nine to five.
questions.explanation: The principle says a request should be granted when all three conditions hold, and only (B) establishes all three: no fixed hours, no missed deadlines in the past six months, and no work shifted to coworkers. (C) is the attractive trap: Lena fails one condition, but the principle says such requests are decided case by case, so it cannot justify denying hers. (A) and (E) each fail a condition outright, and (D) never establishes that Omar has met his deadlines.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If duties don't require fixed hours AND granting won't shift work to coworkers AND the employee met every deadline in the past six months → the request should be granted.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A specific employee's request should be granted (or denied).

breakdown.analysis: Three conditions, all needed, and the rule only tells you when to grant. The last sentence even says that other requests are decided case by case, so the rule never forces a denial. The right answer must show all three conditions and conclude "grant." Failing a sufficient condition doesn't trigger the opposite result. Like "if it's sunny and warm, we'll go to the beach" doesn't tell you you'll stay home if it's cloudy.

choices.note: Fails the coworker condition: coworkers would have to cover her morning calls. With a condition missing, the principle can't justify granting.

CORRECT. Work can be done at any hour (no fixed hours), none of her tasks would fall to her team (no work shifted), and no missed deadline in over a year (covers the past six months). All three conditions hold, so the principle says grant.

Tempting. Lena does miss a condition, so it feels like the rule says no. But the rule only says when to grant, and the policy sends everything else to case-by-case review. A sufficient condition that isn't met tells you nothing.
Never says Omar met his deadlines. Being a "best performer" isn't the same as meeting every deadline. Missing condition.
Fails the fixed-hours condition: he has to staff the front desk nine to five. Can't justify granting.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, amateur astronomers were responsible for about 30 percent of all newly identified asteroids; last year, they were responsible for under 5 percent. Clearly, then, amateurs are finding fewer asteroids than they once did. The likely reason is that light pollution has steadily worsened in the suburbs, where many amateur astronomers live and observe.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on discovery figures from only two years to support a claim about a decade-long trend
presumes, without providing justification, that light pollution affects professional astronomers less severely than it affects amateurs
takes for granted that most amateur astronomers live and observe in suburbs rather than in rural areas
confuses a decline in amateur astronomers’ interest in asteroids with a decline in their observing skill
overlooks the possibility that the total number of asteroids discovered each year has risen sharply
questions.explanation: A falling share of discoveries does not show a falling number: if total discoveries grew enough, for example because professional survey telescopes came online, amateurs could be finding as many asteroids as before or more. (E) identifies this. (A) is tempting, but even many years of shrinking percentages would leave the same gap. (C) misstates the argument, which says only that “many” amateurs live in suburbs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Amateurs are finding fewer asteroids than they once did (likely because of worse light pollution).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ten years ago amateurs found about 30% of newly identified asteroids; last year they found under 5%.

breakdown.analysis: Percent versus number. The evidence is about amateurs' share of discoveries; the conclusion is about how many they find. A share can shrink while the count stays flat or grows, if the total pie gets much bigger. Imagine amateurs found 30 of 100 asteroids then, and 40 of 1,000 now. Their share dropped from 30% to 4%, but they found more. Never jump from a percentage to an absolute number without knowing the total.

choices.note: Tempting, because two data points can be thin. But that isn't the real problem: even with ten years of steadily shrinking percentages, you'd still have the share-versus-number gap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: It rained on my birthday this year and last year, so it always rains on my birthday.

choices.note: The argument doesn't compare how light pollution affects pros versus amateurs. The light-pollution bit is offered only as a likely explanation, and the main flaw is upstream of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smog hurts city runners' times, so it must be why city runners lose to suburban runners, even though we don't know smog affects suburban runners any less.

choices.note: Misreads the argument, which said "many" amateurs live in suburbs, not most. And nothing in the argument hinges on that.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Traffic is bad downtown, so most of our employees must have long commutes, since they surely all live downtown.

choices.note: Interest versus skill never comes up. The argument offers light pollution, not lost interest or lost skill, as a cause.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fewer kids are signing up for piano, so kids today must be worse at music.

choices.note: CORRECT. If total discoveries exploded, say because professional survey telescopes came online, amateurs' share could plunge while their actual count held steady or rose. That's exactly the gap between "under 5 percent" and "fewer asteroids."

questions.stimulus: Food critic: A restaurant’s reputation for freshness depends on its use of ingredients that are in season. But a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients must change that menu several times a year, and frequent menu changes make it hard for a kitchen to prepare dishes consistently. Moreover, diners seldom return to a restaurant whose dishes are inconsistent. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients risks losing its repeat customers
no restaurant can have both a reputation for freshness and a loyal base of repeat customers
restaurants that hope to attract repeat customers should avoid using seasonal ingredients in their dishes
a reputation for freshness is less valuable to a restaurant than one for consistency is
restaurants whose dishes are prepared consistently seldom make use of ingredients that are in season
questions.explanation: The premises connect an all-seasonal menu to frequent changes, frequent changes to difficulty with consistency, and inconsistency to diners not returning, so the cautious conclusion in (A) follows. (B) is the attractive overreach: the critic says only that consistency is hard, not impossible. (C) and (D) add recommendations or rankings the premises do not support, and (E) reverses the direction of the reasoning.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) A freshness reputation depends on using in-season ingredients; 2) an all-seasonal menu must change several times a year; 3) frequent menu changes make consistency hard; 4) diners seldom return to restaurants with inconsistent dishes.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the chain: all-seasonal menu → frequent changes → consistency is hard → (if inconsistent) diners seldom return. Notice the soft spot: "hard," not "impossible." So the honest ending is a risk, not a certainty. Prephrase: a restaurant with an all-seasonal menu risks losing repeat customers. Match the strength of the conclusion to the strength of the premises.

choices.note: CORRECT. It follows the chain and keeps the right strength. All-seasonal menus make consistency hard, and inconsistency drives diners away, so such restaurants risk losing repeat customers.
Too strong. "Hard" isn't "impossible," and a restaurant can lean on seasonal ingredients without building its entire menu around them. "No restaurant can" overreaches.
A recommendation the premises don't support. The problem is building the menu entirely around seasonal ingredients, not using any at all.
Ranks freshness against consistency. The critic never says which is worth more.
This reverses the chain. The premises go from seasonal to inconsistent, not from consistent back to seasonal. Plenty of consistent restaurants could use seasonal ingredients in part of the menu.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Brightline advertises that its LED bulbs last 20 years, a figure based on tests of bulbs in open fixtures at room temperature. But heat shortens the life of LED bulbs, and most household light fixtures are enclosed, trapping heat around the bulb. So in most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the consumer advocate’s argument depends?
choices: Brightline’s competitors base the lifespan claims for their own bulbs on more realistic tests than Brightline uses.
Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is the main cause of the LED bulb failures that occur in most households.
Brightline bulbs are not designed in a way that protects them from the heat trapped in enclosed fixtures.
Bulbs installed in enclosed fixtures fail sooner than bulbs installed in any other kind of household light fixture.
Brightline knew, when it advertised the 20-year figure, that its bulbs would not last that long in most homes.
questions.explanation: The advocate moves from a general fact, that heat shortens LED life, to a prediction about Brightline bulbs in particular. If Brightline bulbs were built to withstand the heat of enclosed fixtures, that prediction would fail, so the argument requires (C). (B) is tempting but too strong: heat need only shorten these bulbs’ lives significantly, not be the leading cause of failure. (D) and (E) are likewise more than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: In most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 20-year claim comes from tests in open fixtures at room temperature; heat shortens LED life; most household fixtures are enclosed and trap heat.

breakdown.analysis: Does a general fact about LEDs have to apply to these LEDs? The advocate goes from "heat shortens LED life" to a prediction about Brightline bulbs. That works only if Brightline bulbs are like typical LEDs in this respect. If Brightline built in a heat sink that shrugs off enclosed-fixture heat, the prediction fails. It's like saying "sun fades fabric, so this awning will fade" without checking whether it's UV-treated. We need an answer that says Brightline bulbs aren't protected. Use the negation test on each choice.

choices.note: Negate it: competitors' tests are just as unrealistic. The argument about Brightline is unaffected. Not required.
choices.negation: Brightline's competitors do not base the lifespan claims for their own bulbs on more realistic tests than Brightline uses.

choices.note: Too strong. Heat only needs to shorten Brightline bulbs' lives a lot, not be the number one cause of failure. Negated, something else is the main cause, but heat could still cut lifespans well short of 20 years. Argument survives.
choices.negation: Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is not the main cause of the LED bulb failures that occur in most households.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, Brightline bulbs are designed to resist enclosed-fixture heat. Then the general fact about heat wouldn't apply to them, and the prediction collapses. Negation wrecks the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Brightline bulbs are designed in a way that protects them from the heat trapped in enclosed fixtures.

choices.note: Too strong. Enclosed fixtures don't have to be the worst kind, just hot enough to shorten life. Negated, some other fixture is even worse, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Bulbs installed in enclosed fixtures do not fail sooner than bulbs installed in every other kind of household light fixture.

choices.note: Intent doesn't matter. The argument is about how long the bulbs last, not whether Brightline knew. Negated, an honest mistake, and the conclusion stands.
choices.negation: Brightline did not know, when it advertised the 20-year figure, that its bulbs would not last that long in most homes.

questions.stimulus: Under a Pelham city ordinance, a food truck may operate downtown only if it holds a downtown permit, and a downtown permit is issued only to trucks that have passed the city’s fire inspection. Moreover, a truck that uses a propane grill passes the fire inspection only if the grill has an automatic shutoff valve.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: A truck that has only ever had a propane grill with no automatic shutoff valve cannot get a downtown permit.
Any food truck that has passed the city’s fire inspection may legally operate anywhere in the downtown area.
Every food truck whose propane grill has an automatic shutoff valve will pass the city’s fire inspection.
A food truck that does not use a propane grill can be issued a downtown permit if it applies for one.
Some of the food trucks that are currently permitted to operate downtown use propane grills to cook their food.
questions.explanation: A permit requires passing inspection, and a truck with a propane grill passes only if the grill has a shutoff valve; a truck whose only grill has never had one could never have passed, so it cannot get a permit, as (A) says. (B) and (C) treat necessary conditions as if they were sufficient, (D) assumes that lacking a propane grill guarantees a permit, and (E) asserts the existence of trucks that the rules never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Operate downtown → downtown permit; 2) downtown permit → passed fire inspection; 3) propane-grill truck passes inspection → grill has automatic shutoff valve.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: operate downtown → permit → passed inspection. For propane trucks, passed inspection → shutoff valve. Contrapositive: propane grill with no shutoff valve → can't pass inspection → no permit → can't operate downtown. All these are necessary conditions. Meeting one doesn't guarantee the next step up. "Only if" introduces what's required, not what's enough. Watch for answers that reverse a link.

choices.note: CORRECT. A truck whose only grill has always been a propane grill without a shutoff valve could never have passed inspection. No pass, no permit. This follows straight from the contrapositive chain.
This reverses the chain. Passing inspection is required for a permit, and a permit is required to operate, but nothing says passing inspection is enough. You still need the permit.
Reverses the last rule. Having a shutoff valve is required to pass, not enough to pass. The truck could fail for some other reason.
Assumes that not using propane is enough to get a permit. The rules never say what guarantees a permit. The truck might still fail inspection.
We don't know this. Conditional rules don't tell you any truck actually operates downtown or what grill it uses.

questions.stimulus: Animal behaviorist: When a pet parrot starts plucking out its own feathers, owners typically assume it is bored and buy it more toys. They would do better to consult an avian veterinarian first. In many cases, plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause: it often begins in parrots that already have plenty of toys and companionship, and it frequently stops after a change in the bird’s diet.
questions.stem: The claim that in many cases plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause plays which one of the following roles in the animal behaviorist’s argument?
choices: It is the argument’s main conclusion, and the observations about toys, companionship, and diet are offered in support of it.
It is a view that the argument presents in order to call it into question by citing evidence that conflicts with it.
It is a premise offered in support of the view that parrots that pluck their own feathers are usually bored.
It is supported by the observations about toys and diet, and it is in turn offered as grounds for the advice to owners.
It is a hypothesis that the argument advances to explain why owners of parrots that pluck tend to buy more toys.
questions.explanation: The main conclusion is the unflagged advice in the middle: owners would do better to consult an avian veterinarian first. The nutritional claim is the reason given for that advice, and it is itself supported by the observations about toys and diet that follow the colon, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (D) says. (A) is the trap: the claim comes last and reads like a thesis, but it is offered as the reason to see a veterinarian, not the other way round. (B) and (E) misdescribe the claim, and (C) has it supporting the boredom view it opposes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Owners of parrots that pluck would do better to consult an avian veterinarian before buying more toys.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plucking often begins in parrots that already have toys and company, and often stops after a diet change; so in many cases it has a nutritional cause; so see a veterinarian first.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the conclusion? Not at the end, and nothing flags it. Ask which statement supports which. Why should owners see a vet first? Because the cause is often nutritional. Why think the cause is nutritional? Because of the toy and diet observations. So the chain is: 1. observations → 2. nutritional cause → 3. see a vet first. The claim in the stem is the middle link: supported, and supporting. Most students pick (A) because the claim comes last, gets direct support after the colon, and sounds like the thesis. It fails because the advice to owners is what the nutritional claim is there to justify. Lesson: position and tone don't make a main conclusion; the support relations do.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The claim sits at the end and gets direct support, so it feels like the point. But ask why the behaviorist tells us the cause is nutritional: to show owners should see a vet before buying toys. That advice is the main conclusion, and it rests on this claim, not the other way round.
Opposite. The argument doesn't question this claim; it argues for it. The view it calls into question is the owners' boredom assumption.
Wrong relation. The nutritional claim cuts against the boredom view; it doesn't support it.
CORRECT. The toy and diet observations support it, and it supports the advice to see a vet first. A claim that is supported and then used as support is an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion.
The claim explains feather plucking, not owners' toy buying. Wrong thing explained.

questions.stimulus: At Kessler Logistics, only employees who have registered a vehicle with security may receive a parking pass, and security registers a vehicle only for an employee who has completed the company’s safety orientation. Dana, a Kessler employee, works only on weekends. It follows that Dana will not receive a parking pass.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every Kessler employee who has completed the safety orientation will receive a parking pass on request.
No Kessler employee who works only on weekends has ever completed the safety orientation.
The safety orientation is offered only on weekdays, when weekend employees are usually not at work.
Most Kessler employees who work only on weekends have not completed the company’s safety orientation.
Employees who work only on weekends rarely drive their own vehicles to Kessler’s offices.
questions.explanation: A pass requires a registered vehicle, and registration requires completing the orientation. If no weekend-only employee has completed it, as (B) states, Dana cannot have a registered vehicle and so cannot receive a pass. (C) is the tempting choice, but a weekday orientation could still have been attended by Dana, perhaps before she switched to weekends. (D) says only “most,” which leaves open that Dana completed it, and (A) reverses the conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dana, who works only on weekends, will not receive a parking pass.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Parking pass → registered vehicle; registered vehicle → completed safety orientation.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: pass → registered → completed orientation. Contrapositive: no orientation → no registration → no pass. To conclude Dana gets no pass, we need Dana to have not completed the orientation. The only thing we know about Dana is that she works only on weekends. Missing link: weekend-only → no orientation completed. It has to be airtight for Dana, so "most" won't do; we need "no weekend-only employee."

choices.note: Reversed. Orientation → pass gives a way to get a pass. We need a way to rule one out.
CORRECT. Weekend-only → no orientation. Dana is weekend-only, so no orientation, so no registered vehicle, so no pass. The conclusion follows for sure.

Tempting. It feels like weekend workers couldn't attend a weekday session. But "usually not at work" leaves room, and Dana might have done it before switching to weekends. Doesn't guarantee she skipped it.
"Most" leaves room for Dana to be in the minority who did complete it. Sufficient assumptions need to guarantee the result, so "most" falls short.
"Rarely drive" doesn't link to the orientation rule at all, and "rarely" isn't "never." Dana might drive and still qualify.

questions.stimulus: Superintendent: Critics claim that moving our high school’s start time from 7:30 to 8:30 has hurt attendance at after-school sports practices, since practices now end after dark for much of the year. But this complaint is unfounded. The number of students on our sports teams this year is actually slightly higher than it was last year, before the change.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the superintendent’s argument?
choices: Some parents have complained that the later start time makes it harder for their children to hold after-school jobs.
During the late fall and winter, most of the school’s teams now finish their practices well after the sun has set.
The school no longer drops students from a team’s roster for missing practices, as it routinely did in previous years.
The number of students on the school’s teams rose more this year than in any of the previous five years.
Practices at neighboring schools that kept a 7:30 start time also end after dark during part of the year.
questions.explanation: The critics’ complaint is about attendance at practices, but the superintendent answers with the number of students on teams. That answer works only if being on a roster still means showing up. (C) breaks that link: if students are no longer dropped for missing practices, rosters can grow while attendance falls. (B) is the trap: it backs up the critics’ reason, but the superintendent never denied that practices end after dark; his point is that no harm followed, and (B) gives no evidence that it did. (D) supports the superintendent, and (A) and (E) do not bear on whether attendance fell.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics' complaint that the later start time hurt attendance at sports practices is unfounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: More students are on the school's sports teams this year than last year, before the change.

breakdown.analysis: So what if more students are on the rosters? The critics talked about attendance at practices. Roster size stands in for attendance only if being on a team means showing up. It's like a gym bragging about its membership count while the weight room sits empty. We need an answer that cuts the link between roster numbers and actual attendance. Most students pick (B) because it seems to back the critics: practices really do end in the dark. It fails because the stimulus already grants that, and the superintendent doesn't deny it. His claim is that the darkness did no harm, and (B) gives no evidence of harm. Lesson: supporting a premise nobody disputes doesn't weaken anything.

choices.note: Different complaint. After-school jobs aren't sports attendance, and this doesn't touch the superintendent's evidence.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like it helps the critics. But the stimulus already says practices end after dark, and the superintendent doesn't dispute it. He argues that it didn't hurt attendance. Repeating the cause isn't showing the effect.

CORRECT. The superintendent's only evidence is roster size. If students now stay on rosters even when they skip practice, a bigger roster says nothing about attendance, which could have dropped. The evidence no longer reaches the conclusion.
This helps the superintendent. A record rise in team membership makes it harder to say the change drove students away.
Other schools' schedules don't tell us whether attendance at this school fell. If anything, it suggests practicing after dark is common.

questions.stimulus: A recent study found that dogs fed from puzzle feeders, which require a dog to work to get its food out, show fewer destructive behaviors at home, such as chewing furniture, than dogs fed from ordinary bowls. The researchers conclude that the mental effort of working out food reduces the boredom that drives much destructive behavior in dogs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers’ argument?
choices: Owners who buy puzzle feeders tend to spend more time exercising their dogs than other dog owners do.
Puzzle feeders slow down dogs’ eating, which can reduce some digestive problems that dogs commonly suffer.
Some of the dogs that were fed from puzzle feeders in the study still chewed furniture when left alone.
Destructive behavior is considerably more common among some breeds of dogs than it is among other breeds.
Dogs that were switched from bowls to puzzle feeders showed fewer destructive behaviors in the following weeks.
questions.explanation: The original evidence compares different dogs, so the difference might reflect the owners or the dogs rather than the feeders. (E) shows the same dogs improving after the switch, which makes the feeder a more likely cause. (A) offers a competing explanation and so weakens; (B) is tempting because it describes another effect of the feeders, but digestion has nothing to do with boredom-driven behavior.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mental effort of working food out of a puzzle feeder reduces the boredom that drives much destructive behavior in dogs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dogs fed from puzzle feeders show fewer destructive behaviors at home than dogs fed from ordinary bowls.

breakdown.analysis: Different dogs, different owners. Maybe puzzle-feeder owners are just more attentive, or their dogs are calmer to begin with. The best strengthener isolates the feeder. One clean way: same dogs, before and after switching. If the same dog gets better after the switch, it's hard to blame the owner or the breed. Like testing new glasses: if you see better right after putting them on, it wasn't your eyes changing.

choices.note: Weakens. Puzzle-feeder owners exercise their dogs more, and exercise could be why their dogs are less destructive. A rival cause.
Tempting because it's another real benefit of puzzle feeders. But digestion has nothing to do with boredom. Doesn't help the boredom explanation.
"Some" dogs still chew furniture. That's consistent with a reduction overall, and if anything it slightly hurts. Doesn't strengthen.
Breed differences only matter if the feeder group had different breeds, and this doesn't say so. At most it hints at a rival cause. Doesn't strengthen.

CORRECT. Same dogs, switched from bowls to puzzle feeders, fewer destructive behaviors afterward. That rules out "different dogs" or "different owners" as the explanation and makes the feeder look like the cause.

questions.stimulus: Hester Vane’s diary, which she kept while living in Millbrook from 1843 to 1849, describes her crossing a covered bridge over the Tull River. The diary also records her frequent trips to other towns along the Tull. Yet Millbrook’s earliest map, a detailed survey drawn in 1852, shows no bridge over the river. So the bridge Vane described must have been in one of those other towns.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Did Vane make any trips to towns other than Millbrook during the years in which she was keeping her diary?
Were the bridges built over the Tull River during the 1840s generally still standing by the year 1852?
Were covered bridges in the 1840s considerably more expensive to build than bridges that were not covered?
Was the 1852 survey of Millbrook paid for by the town’s government or by a group of private landowners?
Did other residents of Millbrook keep diaries during the 1840s that have survived to the present day?
questions.explanation: The only evidence against a Millbrook bridge is the 1852 map, drawn a few years after the diary. That evidence counts only if a bridge from the 1840s would probably still have been there in 1852. (B) asks exactly that: if such bridges usually lasted, the map’s silence is telling; if they often washed out or fell down within a few years, it tells us little. (A) is the trap: it raises the possibility that Vane crossed the bridge elsewhere, but the argument already states that she traveled often to other towns, so its answer adds nothing. (C), (D), and (E) do not bear on where the bridge stood.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bridge Vane described was in another town along the Tull, not in Millbrook.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Vane's 1840s diary describes crossing a covered bridge over the Tull; she often traveled to other river towns; Millbrook's detailed 1852 map shows no bridge.

breakdown.analysis: So what if there's no bridge on an 1852 map? Vane was writing in the 1840s, and a map shows only what stood when it was drawn. It's like concluding your town never had a drive-in theater because this year's map doesn't show one. The argument needs a bridge that existed in the 1840s to still be around in 1852. We need a question whose answer tells us whether that's likely. Most students pick (A) because their prephrase is "maybe she crossed it somewhere else." It fails because the stimulus already tells us she traveled to other river towns often. A question the argument has already answered can't help you evaluate it.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's the natural first thought. But the argument already says she made frequent trips to other towns. The answer to this question is given, so it can't change how strong the argument is.

CORRECT. If 1840s bridges usually stood for years, a bridge in Millbrook should have shown up on the 1852 map, and the argument gets stronger. If they often washed away or collapsed within a few years, the map's silence means little, and the argument falls apart. Either answer matters.
Cost has nothing to do with where this bridge stood. Irrelevant.
Who paid for the survey doesn't tell us whether an earlier bridge survived until it was drawn. The argument already grants that it's a detailed survey.
Whether other diaries survived tells us nothing unless we know what they say. And the real gap is the time between the diary and the map.

questions.stimulus: Most of the buildings on Market Street date from before 1900, and most of the city’s buildings that date from before 1900 have been designated as historic landmarks. So most of the buildings on Market Street have been designated as historic landmarks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most houses on Quarry Lane were built before 1900, and every house in the city built before 1900 has been designated a historic landmark. So most houses on Quarry Lane have been designated historic landmarks.
Most members of the town choir are sopranos, and most of the choir’s sopranos also play a musical instrument. So at least some members of the town choir play a musical instrument.
No member of the Ridgeview hiking club smokes, and most members of the hiking club are also runners. So most of the runners who live in the area do not smoke.
More than half of the paintings in the east gallery must be on loan, since more than half of them are oils and more than half of the museum’s oils are on loan.
Most of the apples grown on the Garza farm are sold at the farmers’ market each fall. So most of the produce grown on the Garza farm is sold at the farmers’ market.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two “most” statements as if they guaranteed overlap, but the Market Street buildings could fall among the pre-1900 buildings that are not landmarks. (D) makes the same move with paintings, oils, and loans, though it states its conclusion first and says “more than half” instead of “most.” (A) is the trap: it copies the stimulus’s topic and wording, but its second premise says “every,” so its conclusion follows. (B) is also valid, since it concludes only “some.” (C) and (E) are flawed, but in different ways.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most buildings on Market Street have been designated historic landmarks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most Market Street buildings date from before 1900; most of the city's pre-1900 buildings are landmarks.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C (invalid: the A's may be the B's that aren't C).

breakdown.analysis: Is "most" plus "most" enough? No. Imagine the city has 1,000 pre-1900 buildings, 600 of them landmarks. Market Street has 100 buildings, 60 of them pre-1900, and all 60 could be among the 400 that aren't landmarks. "Most" isn't "all": the buildings you care about could be the other ones. We need an answer with the same two "most" links and a "most" conclusion. Most students pick (A) because it looks like a copy: old buildings, 1900, landmarks. It fails because its middle premise says "every," which makes it valid. Match the structure, not the topic, and don't be thrown when the right answer leads with its conclusion and says "more than half" for "most."

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Same topic, same order, almost the same words. But every house built before 1900 is a landmark, so most Quarry Lane houses must be landmarks. That's valid; the original's error is gone.
Valid, so not a match. The sopranos are choir members, so if most of them play an instrument, at least some choir members do. The modest "some" conclusion follows.
Flawed, but differently. It jumps from facts about club members to a claim about all runners in the area. That's a shift in group, not a "most + most" chain.

CORRECT. Rearranged: most east-gallery paintings are oils; most of the museum's oils are on loan; so most east-gallery paintings are on loan. Same two "mosts," same overreaching "most" conclusion. The east-gallery oils could be the museum's oils that stayed home.
Flawed, but differently: it moves from one kind of produce (apples) to all produce. That's a part-to-whole move with one premise, not a chain.

questions.stimulus: Councilor Reyes: Supporters of the proposed bus-only lane on Garnet Avenue claim that it will cut commute times for bus riders, because a similar lane in Easton did so. But buses in Easton run twice as often as ours do, so Easton’s results tell us little about what would happen on Garnet Avenue. Hence, the bus lane will not cut commute times for our riders.
questions.stem: The reasoning in Councilor Reyes’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on a comparison between two cities that differ in a respect that bears on the conclusion being drawn
attacks the motives of the lane’s supporters rather than addressing the reasons they offer for the proposal
presumes, without providing justification, that bus frequency is the only factor that affects the length of riders’ commutes
overlooks the possibility that a bus-only lane on Garnet Avenue would also benefit people who drive their own cars
infers that a prediction is false from the fact that the evidence offered in support of that prediction is weak
questions.explanation: Reyes fairly shows that the Easton comparison is weak support for the lane, but then concludes that the lane will not cut commute times. A poorly supported prediction may still come true, so (E) names the flaw. (A) is the trap: the shaky comparison belongs to the supporters, and pointing it out is the sound part of Reyes’s reasoning, not something Reyes relies on. (C) misreads frequency as Reyes’s only factor, and (B) and (D) describe moves Reyes never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bus lane will not cut commute times for Garnet Avenue riders.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Supporters cite Easton's bus lane; but Easton's buses run twice as often, so Easton's results tell us little about Garnet Avenue.

breakdown.analysis: Reyes does something fair, then something unfair. Fair: Easton is a weak comparison, so the supporters' evidence is weak. Unfair: concluding that the lane won't work. So what if their evidence is bad? Weak evidence for a claim isn't evidence against it. It's like saying "Your only reason for thinking it'll rain is that your knee hurts, which is silly, so it won't rain." It still might. Most students pick (A) because they spot a weak analogy in the stimulus and grab the answer that names one. It fails because Reyes isn't relying on the analogy; Reyes is knocking it down. Know whose argument you're critiquing. Knocking down an argument doesn't prove the opposite.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. There is a shaky comparison here, but it belongs to the supporters. Reyes points it out, which is the sound part of the argument. Reyes isn't the one relying on it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Rome's new subway was a huge success, so our town of 5,000 should build a subway too.

choices.note: Reyes never says anything about why supporters want the lane. The attack is on their evidence, not their motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The developer says the new mall will help the town, but he'd make millions from it, so his argument is worthless.

choices.note: Tempting, but Reyes treats bus frequency as one relevant difference that undermines the comparison, not as the only thing that matters for commute times.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our buses run as often as Easton's, so our commute times must be just like theirs.

choices.note: The argument is about bus riders' commutes. Whether drivers benefit is beside the point.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A new park won't help children, since adults are the ones who'll use the walking trails.

choices.note: CORRECT. The "prediction" is that the lane will cut commute times; the weak evidence is the Easton comparison. Reyes shows the evidence is weak, then concludes the prediction is false. A poorly supported claim can still be true.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant reviewer: Café Morrow’s menu used to state that its bread was baked in-house. When the café began buying its bread from a local bakery, it simply removed that statement. Some diners complain that the café should have announced the change. But the café never made a false claim; it merely stopped making a true claim once the claim became false. So the café did nothing wrong.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the restaurant reviewer’s argument?
choices: Diners are entitled to know where each item that a restaurant serves them was made, unless telling them would be costly.
A business does nothing wrong in changing its suppliers as long as the quality of what it sells stays the same.
A business’s failure to tell its customers about a change is not wrong unless it results in the business’s making a false statement.
Any business that makes a false claim about its products has wronged its customers, whether or not anyone was harmed.
Whether a business has wronged its customers depends entirely on whether any of those customers was actually harmed.
questions.explanation: The reviewer’s defense is that the café never said anything false, since it dropped the in-house claim when the claim stopped being true. (C) turns that into a rule: keeping quiet about a change is wrong only if it leads to a false statement, which did not happen here, so the café did nothing wrong. (D) is the trap: it links false claims to wrongdoing, which sounds like the reviewer’s point, but it says only what follows when a false claim is made, and the café made none. (B) depends on bread quality, which the argument never discusses, (E) depends on harm, and (A) supports the diners.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Café Morrow did nothing wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Diners say the café should have announced its switch to bakery bread; but the café never made a false claim; it just stopped making a true claim once it became false.

breakdown.analysis: Why does "never said anything false" clear the café? Only if saying something false is the way you'd go wrong here. Keeping quiet about a change has to be fine as long as nothing you say turns into a lie. We need a principle like: not announcing a change isn't wrong unless it leaves you making a false statement. Most students pick (D) because it puts "false claim" and "wronged" in one sentence, which looks like the reviewer's logic. But (D) says false claim → wrong. The café made no false claim, and that rule says nothing about cases without one. Reading it as "no false claim → no wrong" reverses it. A principle-justify answer has to deliver the conclusion the author reached.

choices.note: Opposite. This sides with the diners: they'd be entitled to be told the bread now came from elsewhere.
It turns on quality, which the reviewer never mentions. And the diners' complaint is about the missing announcement, not the switch itself.

CORRECT. Not telling diners is wrong only if it leads the café into a false statement. The café removed the in-house claim, so it said nothing false. The rule then says its silence wasn't wrong, which is the reviewer's conclusion.

Tempting, and the main trap. False claim → wronged customers. The café made no false claim, so the rule never triggers and can't tell us the café did nothing wrong. Taking "no false claim" to mean "no wrong" reverses the rule.
The reviewer never mentions harm. This principle would need facts we don't have, and it isn't the reviewer's reason.

questions.stimulus: Astronomy club president: Some members want us to double the number of public stargazing nights, since attendance has been strong. But the program depends entirely on a handful of volunteers who bring and operate their own telescopes, and several of them say they are already stretched thin. Expanding in a way that drives those volunteers away would end the program altogether. So we should not double the number of nights.
questions.stem: The principle underlying the argument above is most similar to the principle underlying which one of the following arguments?
choices: Restaurant owner: Our lunch special is very popular, but we lose money on every one we serve. So we should raise its price, even if that means fewer customers will order it.
School principal: Some parents want us to add field trips. But each trip uses money that would otherwise go to new books, and our book budget is already tight. So we should not add field trips.
Library director: Our volunteer tutors tell us they greatly enjoy their work, and many say they would gladly do more. So we can extend tutoring hours without hiring any paid staff.
Mayor: The farmers market has become very crowded. It should move to a larger lot, even though vendors there would pay higher fees, because the extra customers would more than make up the difference.
Garden coordinator: Neighbors want a second garden plot. But our garden depends on a few retirees who already feel overworked, and if they quit, the garden would end. So we should not add the plot.
questions.explanation: The president’s principle is that an activity should not be expanded if expanding it would likely drive off the few people it depends on and so end it entirely. (E) applies the same principle to a garden kept up by overworked retirees. (B) is the closest trap, but it rests on a budget tradeoff between two goods, not on losing the people who make the activity possible; (C) shares the volunteer theme but reaches the opposite kind of conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The club should not double the number of public stargazing nights.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The program depends entirely on a few volunteers who are already stretched thin; expanding in a way that drives them away would end the program.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: People want to expand X; X depends entirely on a few overstretched people; losing them would end X; so don't expand X.

breakdown.analysis: The principle: don't grow something if growing it would burn out the few people it can't survive without. Find the answer with the same logic: demand to expand, a small overworked group the whole thing depends on, and the risk of losing everything. Don't get pulled in by a choice that just says no to an expansion for some other reason.
