choices.note: Different principle entirely: a money-losing item should have its price raised. No expansion request, no fragile group of people.
Tempting. It also says "don't expand," but the reason is a budget tradeoff (field trips vs. books), not losing the people who keep the program alive.
Shares the volunteer theme but goes the other way: volunteers are happy, so expand. Different reasoning and opposite conclusion.
This argues for expanding (moving to a bigger lot) because the benefits outweigh the costs. Nothing about a small group of people the market depends on.
CORRECT. Neighbors want more; the garden depends on a few overworked retirees; if they quit there's no garden; so don't add the plot. Same principle, same structure.

questions.stimulus: Of the customers who bought the Tallis desk chair from Orrin Office Supply last year, most also bought the optional lumbar cushion. Of those customers who returned the chair, however, most had not bought the cushion. No customer bought more than one Tallis chair, and every return was made by a customer who had bought the chair last year.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the customers who bought the Tallis chair last year without the lumbar cushion later returned the chair.
Buying the optional lumbar cushion made customers less likely than they otherwise would have been to return their chairs.
More Tallis chairs were returned by customers who bought the lumbar cushion than by customers who did not.
Customers who bought the lumbar cushion kept their Tallis chairs at a higher rate than customers who did not.
Most of the customers who bought the Tallis chair from Orrin Office Supply last year did not return it.
questions.explanation: Most buyers took the cushion, yet most returns came from buyers who did not. A smaller group producing more returns must have a higher return rate, so cushion buyers kept their chairs at a higher rate, which is (D) stated from the other side. (B) is the trap: it reads the rate difference as the cushion’s effect, but the data show only a correlation; customers who skipped the cushion may differ in other ways. (A) and (E) need the overall return rate, which is not given, and (C) contradicts the second statement.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most Tallis chair buyers also bought the cushion; 2. Most customers who returned the chair had not bought the cushion; 3. One chair per customer, and every return came from last year's buyers.

breakdown.analysis: This is a rate-versus-count puzzle. Say 100 people bought the chair: 70 with the cushion, 30 without. If most returns came from the no-cushion group, that smaller group produced more returns than the bigger one. So its return rate is higher, and the cushion group's keep rate is higher. That's the safe inference, but watch the phrasing: the right answer says it from the "kept" side. Most students pick (B) because the numbers seem to show the cushion working. It fails because the facts show only a difference between groups, not a cause. Maybe people who buy add-ons are people who had already decided they love the chair.

choices.note: We don't know this. With 30 no-cushion buyers, maybe only 3 returned and 2 cushion buyers returned. Most returns would still be no-cushion, yet only 10% of that group returned.
Tempting, and the main trap. It turns a correlation into a cause. The facts show who returned chairs, not why. Buyers who skip the add-on might be less committed to the chair from the start.
This contradicts fact 2. Most returns came from customers without the cushion, so they returned more chairs.
CORRECT. The no-cushion group is smaller (fact 1) but produced more returns (fact 2), so its return rate is higher. Flip it: cushion buyers kept their chairs at a higher rate.
Could be true, but nothing says so. The facts compare the two groups; they never tell us how many returns there were overall.

passages.title: Serial Publication and the Victorian Novel
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers began appearing in monthly parts in 1836, it helped establish a mode of publication that would shape British fiction for decades: the novel issued in installments, in separate numbers or in magazines. The literary historian Ines Varga has argued that many features for which Victorian novels were long criticized are best understood as products of this mode. Suspenseful endings of installments, proliferating subplots, and the habit of tagging minor characters with a signature phrase are, on Varga’s account, not lapses of craft but rational responses to what she calls “serial form.” She has little patience for earlier critics who dismissed such features as “padding paid for by the page,” a judgment she describes as mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures.

Varga’s account is persuasive in outline, but it fails to clarify what serial form is supposed to have demanded. In her usage the term does double duty. Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers, who met a novel in fragments weeks apart and needed reminders of who was who. At other times it refers to the situation of writers, many of whom composed each installment shortly before it was due and could not revise chapters already in print. These are distinct pressures, and they predict different things: the first should leave its mark wherever readers encountered a text intermittently, however it was written; the second, wherever a text was written under deadline, however it was read.

Varga’s evidence, moreover, rests on a comparison whose significance she does not establish. She shows that the features in question are markedly more common in serialized novels than in novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries. But the comparison is telling only if the two groups are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are. If publishers offered serialization chiefly to established popular authors, whose habits of plotting predated their first serials, or to comic and sensational stories, in which suspense and broadly drawn characters were old conventions, the difference she documents may owe less to the mode of publication than to the authors and stories it attracted.

The novelist Edmund Carrow complicates matters further. Carrow finished each of his novels before its first installment appeared, yet his books abound in cliffhangers and in minor characters identified by recurring tics. Varga treats Carrow as confirming her thesis, since he wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts. Perhaps so—but his novels contain almost none of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail that she also attributes to serial form. Carrow thus suggests that the two pressures her term conflates operated independently. Varga has identified a real cause; what her account needs is a finer description of how that cause worked.

passages.title: Unbalanced accounts in the Orlen Valley ledgers
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
When the household account books kept by farming families in the Orlen Valley between roughly 1780 and 1860 were first catalogued in the 1950s, archivists noticed a curious feature. Entries recording loans of grain, labor, and tools between neighboring households almost never balance. When such a debt was repaid, the repayment was nearly always a little more or a little less than the original loan, and the difference was carried forward rather than settled. Early commentators took this as evidence of careless bookkeeping, or of a rural population that lacked the arithmetic to reconcile its accounts.

The anthropologist Teodora Halvik has offered a different explanation. In her view, the imbalances were deliberate. Among Orlen households, she argues, an exchange that ended with nothing owed on either side ended the relationship as well; to repay a neighbor exactly was to announce that one no longer wished to be bound to that neighbor. Keeping a small remainder perpetually outstanding was thus a way of keeping the relationship open. Halvik notes that the ledgers have a local expression for such an account: it is said to be “on the long thread.”

Halvik’s evidence is of several kinds. The same households that left their neighbors’ accounts unbalanced kept precise records of their dealings with grain merchants from outside the valley, and those accounts were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete. Nor were the remainders random: they were small, typically less than a tenth of the original loan, and the direction of the imbalance tended to alternate, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor. Finally, in the few cases in which an account between neighbors was closed exactly, parish records from the same months frequently note a dispute between the two families, a lawsuit, or the departure of one of them from the valley.

The ledger of the Brenn household illustrates the mechanism. In the spring of 1812 the Brenns lent twelve bushels of rye to the neighboring Tamm family. At harvest the Tamms returned thirteen, leaving the Brenns owing the Tamms one bushel. That winter the Brenns repaid the bushel with two days of labor on the Tamms’ threshing floor—work the ledger values at slightly more than a bushel, so that the Tamms now owed the Brenns a small fraction. The account continued in this way, alternating, for thirty-one years, and was closed only in 1843, the year in which the parish register records a quarrel over a boundary stone between the two families. If Halvik is right, the ledgers are not failed attempts at reckoning but successful records of a different kind: they tracked not merely what was owed but who remained bound to whom.

passages.title: Court-Appointed Expert Witnesses
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In most common-law jurisdictions a trial judge may, on a party’s motion or on the judge’s own initiative, appoint an expert witness of the court’s choosing. The power is seldom used, and its advocates attribute this to judicial timidity. There are, however, sound reasons for the reluctance.

First, an expert introduced to the jury as the court’s own arrives cloaked in a neutrality that no party’s expert can match. Jurors told that one witness was chosen by the judge are apt to treat that witness’s opinion not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified, so that a single person who was never meant to decide the case effectively does so.

Second, the appointment itself is far from neutral. In fields where the science is unsettled—the reliability of certain forensic techniques, say, or the causes of a rare illness—competent specialists disagree, and to select one of them is to select a side. A judge, who by hypothesis lacks the expertise to resolve the dispute, is poorly placed to recognize that a choice of person is also a choice of doctrine, and the jury will never learn that such a choice was made at all.

Third, the court’s expert is shielded from the testing that adversarial procedure supplies. A lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge’s own witness risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk. The remedy for partisan expertise is not to abandon the adversarial method but to strengthen it: earlier disclosure of expert reports, and pretrial hearings at which opposing experts must confront each other’s reasoning.

Passage B

Litigants do not hire experts at random. They interview several and retain the one whose views best serve their case—or whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it. The result in a technical dispute is often two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable, presented to jurors who have no basis for choosing between them. Studies with mock jurors suggest that in such contests jurors tend to credit whichever expert seems more poised and likable, a standard unrelated to the merits.

A court-appointed expert addresses this problem not by replacing the parties’ experts but by giving jurors a fixed point against which to measure them. The parties remain free to call their own witnesses and to cross-examine the court’s. And if jurors give the court’s expert more weight than either party’s, that is hardly a defect: an expert chosen for competence rather than for persuasiveness deserves more weight.

Nor need the selection be left to a judge’s unaided guesswork. Courts can ask each side to nominate candidates and appoint someone acceptable to both, or can ask a professional body to propose a panel. Where a field is genuinely divided, the appointed expert can be instructed to report the range of respectable opinion rather than only her own. And the judge should tell jurors plainly that the court’s expert is a witness like any other, whose testimony they may accept or reject.

passages.title: Recruitment failure in the slate pearlmussel
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In the early twentieth century the slate pearlmussel was among the most abundant freshwater mussels in the Halder River. By the 1970s, however, surveys upstream of the Ostrow Dam, which had been completed in 1931, were finding fewer of the mussels each decade, and the decline was attributed to the industrial pollution and agricultural sediment that had degraded much of the river. A regional cleanup program begun in 1978 cut discharges sharply, and by the late 1980s water quality above the dam met every standard the program had set. The mussels continued to decline.

In 1994 the biologist Renata Kovač proposed that the problem lay not in the water but in the mussel’s life cycle. Like many freshwater mussels, the slate pearlmussel cannot complete its development on its own. A female releases larvae, called glochidia, that must clamp onto the gills of a fish, where they become encapsulated in its tissue and live as parasites for several weeks before dropping off as juvenile mussels. Kovač found that glochidia exposed in the laboratory to a dozen fish species transformed successfully only on the Halder herring, a migratory fish that once ascended the river each spring to spawn; on other species they were shed within days. The dam, which had no fish passage, had ended the herring’s runs. Kovač then aged living mussels by counting the annual growth rings on their shells. Downstream of the dam, mussels of every age were present; upstream, nearly all were more than sixty-five years old—older, that is, than the dam itself. Because adults can live for most of a century, she argued, the upstream population had been reproductively dead for decades while appearing merely diminished.

Kovač urged that funds be redirected from further water-quality measures to fish passage at the dam, and her proposal met resistance. Some biologists objected that laboratory results might not reflect conditions in the river, where glochidia might use hosts that fare poorly in tanks. Others noted that the dam had also caused fine sediment to accumulate above it, and that juvenile mussels, which burrow and feed in the riverbed, are more sensitive to such sediment than adults are. The missing age classes, these critics argued, might reflect where juveniles could survive rather than whether they were being produced.

A fish lift began operating at the dam in 2008. Within two years, herring caught upstream were found carrying encysted glochidia, and surveys in 2015 recovered juvenile pearlmussels above the dam for the first time in living memory—including in reaches where sediment had not measurably changed. Recruitment was nonetheless markedly lower in the siltiest reaches, suggesting that Kovač’s critics had identified a real, though secondary, constraint. The episode is now often cited as a caution: a population of long-lived adults can conceal a failure of reproduction for generations.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Varga has shown that features of Victorian novels that earlier critics dismissed as flaws of craft were in fact rational responses to the demands of serial publication.
Varga’s account of the influence of serial publication on the Victorian novel is undermined by the case of a novelist who completed his books before serializing them.
Although Varga is right that serial publication shaped the Victorian novel, her account conflates two distinct pressures and rests on a comparison whose significance is uncertain.
The features of Victorian serialized novels are better explained by the pressures that serial publication placed on writers than by those it placed on readers.
Varga’s comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete overlooks differences between the kinds of authors and stories in the two groups.
questions.explanation: The author calls Varga's account 'persuasive in outline' (second paragraph) and ends by saying she 'has identified a real cause' (fourth paragraph), but argues that her term conflates two pressures (second and fourth paragraphs) and that her comparison rests on an unexamined assumption (third paragraph), so C is correct. A states Varga's view without the author's reservations. B is the most tempting trap: the Carrow case 'complicates matters' but the author never says it undermines Varga's thesis. D picks one pressure over the other, and E is a single point from the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position: what the author grants Varga and what the author faults in her account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (Varga's thesis), paragraph 2 ('persuasive in outline, but ...'), paragraph 3 (the comparison), and the last sentence of paragraph 4 ('a real cause ... a finer description').

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for Varga or against her? Both. The author grants the big claim (serial publication really did shape these novels) and then lists two problems: the term 'serial form' blurs readers' and writers' pressures, and the comparison with novels issued complete assumes the two groups are otherwise alike. The last sentence sums it up: a real cause that needs a finer description. We need an answer that says 'Varga is basically right, but her account is muddled in these ways.' A partly-favorable-with-reservations main point is classic LSAT.

choices.note: This is Varga's own view with the author's reservations stripped out. 'Has shown' is far stronger than 'persuasive in outline.'

Tempting, because Carrow is a problem case. But the author says Carrow 'complicates matters' and refines the account; it doesn't undermine it. The last sentence still says Varga 'has identified a real cause.' Too strong.
CORRECT. Concession ('right that serial publication shaped the Victorian novel') plus both criticisms (the conflated pressures of paragraphs 2 and 4, the uncertain comparison of paragraph 3).
The author never ranks writers' pressures above readers'. The point is that both operated, separately. This invents a winner.
True to paragraph 3, but it's one supporting point. A main point has to cover the double-duty problem and the concession too.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the novels with which Varga compares serialized novels were
choices: typically issued in three volumes for the circulating libraries
written chiefly by established popular authors whose habits of plotting predated serialization
composed in installments but published only after the last installment was finished
more likely than serialized novels to end their chapters with suspenseful scenes
the main target of the earlier critics who dismissed certain features as padding
questions.explanation: The second sentence of the third paragraph says Varga compares serialized novels with 'novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries,' which is A. B is the trap: it borrows the passage's hypothesis about which authors received serialization and attaches it to the wrong group, and even then the passage offers it only as an 'if.' D reverses Varga's finding, and C and E are never said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the comparison group: the novels Varga sets against serialized ones.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence ('novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries').

breakdown.analysis: A straight detail question. Go back to where the comparison is described and read the exact words: the other group is novels 'first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries.' Prephrase: three-volume novels for the libraries. The traps will reuse words from the next sentences of the same paragraph and pin them on the wrong group.

choices.note: CORRECT. A near-verbatim match to the second sentence of paragraph 3.

Tempting, since 'established popular authors, whose habits of plotting predated their first serials' appears in paragraph 3. But that phrase is about who got serialized (the other group), and it's only an 'if.' Wrong group, and stated as fact when the passage only supposes it.
Nothing says this. It sounds like Carrow's practice (paragraph 4), but Carrow's novels were serialized, so he isn't in the comparison group at all.
Reversed. Varga shows the features, cliffhangers included, are 'markedly more common in serialized novels.'
The earlier critics (paragraph 1) dismissed features of Victorian novels generally. The passage never says they targeted the novels issued complete.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s attitude toward the judgment of earlier critics that certain features of Victorian novels were “padding paid for by the page” can best be described as one of
choices: indifference
sympathy
ambivalence
deference
disapproval
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says Varga 'has little patience' for those critics and calls their judgment a case of 'mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures,' which is disapproval (E). C is the likeliest trap for readers who notice the author's own reservations about Varga, but those belong to the author; Varga is never described as torn about the critics. A, B, and D are contradicted by her impatience.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Name Varga's attitude (not the author's) toward the earlier critics' 'padding' judgment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence ('has little patience for earlier critics ... mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures').

breakdown.analysis: Whose attitude? Varga's. Don't mix her up with the author, who has mixed feelings about Varga. The passage says Varga 'has little patience' for the critics and says they mistook the conditions of an art for its failures. That's a clear negative. Prephrase: she disapproves.

choices.note: No. 'Has little patience' means she cares enough to reject it.
Opposite. She thinks the critics got it wrong.
Tempting if you blend Varga with the author. The author is mixed about Varga; Varga isn't mixed about the critics.
Opposite. She dismisses their judgment rather than deferring to it.
CORRECT. 'Little patience' plus calling their view a mistake is disapproval.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “does double duty” (second sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that Varga’s term “serial form”
choices: serves both to explain certain features of Victorian novels and to defend those features against earlier critics
is applied, without distinction, to two different sets of circumstances that might have shaped the novels
covers both novels issued in separate monthly numbers and novels serialized in magazines
is used both by Varga and by the earlier critics whose judgments about the novels she rejects
names both the characteristic features of serialized novels and the conditions that produced those features
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the phrase: 'sometimes' the term refers to readers' situation and 'at other times' to writers', and the author calls these 'distinct pressures,' so B is correct. A is the strongest trap because Varga's account does both explain and defend the features, but the second paragraph is about what the term refers to, not about the uses of her account. C draws on the two formats named in the first sentence of the first paragraph, which the author never says the term blurs. D and E have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what 'does double duty' means here, using the sentences around it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 2-5 (readers' situation 'sometimes,' writers' situation 'at other times,' 'distinct pressures').

breakdown.analysis: Don't answer from the dictionary sense ('serves two purposes'). Read the next sentences: the term sometimes means readers' situation, at other times writers' situation, and these are 'distinct pressures' that 'predict different things.' So the complaint is that one term covers two different things without telling them apart. We need an answer about two sets of circumstances lumped together.

choices.note: Tempting. Varga's account does explain and defend the features. But 'double duty' is about what the term refers to (readers vs. writers), not about two jobs her argument does.
CORRECT. Two different situations (readers' and writers'), one undifferentiated term. 'Without distinction' captures why it's a criticism.
Recycles 'separate numbers or in magazines' from paragraph 1. The author never says the term blurs those two formats, and that wouldn't matter to the argument.
Nothing says the earlier critics used the term. It's Varga's coinage ('what she calls').
Not supported. The two things the term covers are both conditions (readers' and writers' situations), not a feature plus a condition.

questions.stem: The author mentions “comic and sensational stories” (last sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: identify the kinds of fiction for which publishers first adopted the practice of issuing novels in monthly installments
suggest that the earlier critics’ dismissal of certain features as padding was justified at least for some kinds of fiction
illustrate the pressures that serial publication placed on readers who encountered novels in fragments weeks apart
point to a way in which the novels that Varga compares might differ other than in mode of publication
show that suspenseful endings and broadly drawn characters were more common in novels issued complete than in serialized ones
questions.explanation: The phrase sits in an 'if' clause naming ways the two groups Varga compares might not be 'otherwise alike': if serialization went chiefly to genres in which suspense and broadly drawn characters were already conventions, her finding could reflect genre rather than publication mode. That is D. C is tempting because suspense and memorable characters relate to readers' needs, but this paragraph is about the makeup of the comparison groups. A states a history the passage never gives, B is unsupported, and E reverses Varga's finding.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up comic and sensational stories.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, especially the third sentence ('telling only if the two groups are otherwise alike') and the last sentence ('If publishers offered serialization chiefly to ...').

breakdown.analysis: What job does the example do? Paragraph 3 says Varga's comparison only proves something if serialized novels and complete novels are alike apart from how they were published. Then the 'if' sentence gives two ways they might not be alike: who wrote them (established authors) and what kind of stories they were (comic and sensational). So the example is a possible confound. Prephrase: to show the groups might differ in genre, not just publication mode.

choices.note: The passage makes no claim about which fiction was serialized first. It only supposes, with 'if,' who received serialization.
Nothing here vindicates the old critics. The point is about Varga's evidence, not about whether the features are padding.
Tempting, since suspense and memorable characters connect to readers' needs (paragraph 2). But paragraph 3 isn't about readers; it's about whether the two groups are comparable.
CORRECT. Genre is a difference between the two groups other than mode of publication, which is exactly what would make the comparison misleading.
Reversed. Varga found these features more common in serialized novels, and the author doesn't dispute the numbers.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s interpretation of Carrow’s novels commits her to which one of the following views?
choices: Some features she attributes to serial form can appear in a novel whose author was not writing against installment deadlines.
The abandoned subplots found in many serialized novels arose from the conditions under which those novels were written rather than read.
The term “serial form” should be reserved for the situation of readers who met novels in installments weeks apart.
Carrow’s novels contain as many abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail as do novels written installment by installment.
Novelists who completed their work before serialization were more skilled at plotting than those who wrote installment by installment.
questions.explanation: Carrow finished each novel before its first installment appeared, so he wrote under no installment deadline, yet Varga counts his cliffhangers and tic-tagged characters as confirming her thesis (fourth paragraph). She is therefore committed to A: some serial-form features can arise without deadline composition. B is the dominant trap: it is the author’s inference from Carrow’s lack of abandoned subplots, an opinion Varga never expresses; her term ‘conflates’ the two pressures. C is too strong, D contradicts the fourth paragraph, and E introduces a ranking of skill no one in the passage makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what Varga must believe, given that she counts Carrow as support for her thesis. Not what the author concludes about Carrow: what Varga is stuck with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2–3 (Carrow finished his novels first; Varga treats him as confirming her thesis 'since he wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts'). Contrast sentence 4 onward, which is the author talking.

breakdown.analysis: Carrow had no deadlines: every book was done before installment one. Yet his books have cliffhangers and tic-tagged minor characters, features Varga credits to serial form. So if she says Carrow confirms her thesis, what is she stuck with? That those features can show up without deadline writing. We need an answer that says: serial-form features can arise even when the writer wasn't racing the printer. Most students pick (B) because it is the lesson of the Carrow paragraph. It is, but it's the author's lesson. The author separates writing-pressure features (abandoned subplots) from reading-pressure features (cliffhangers); Varga's term lumps them together. Separate whose view is whose before you answer a 'commits her to' question.

choices.note: CORRECT. Counting Carrow's cliffhangers and tics as serial-form effects means accepting that such features can arise in a book not composed against deadlines. Note the hedge: 'some features ... can appear.' That's all her reading requires.

Tempting. This is the trap. It's what the author infers from Carrow ('almost none of the abandoned subplots'), and it may well be true. But Varga never assigns abandoned subplots to the writing side as opposed to the reading side; the passage says her term 'conflates' the two. Her Carrow reading doesn't commit her to splitting them.
Too strong. Accepting a reader-side effect in Carrow doesn't commit her to dropping the writer side of her term. She still blames serial form for abandoned subplots and inconsistencies too.
Contradicted. Paragraph 4 says Carrow's novels contain 'almost none' of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies.
Nothing about relative skill. Varga's whole approach treats these features as responses to conditions, not as marks of more or less talent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Orlen Valley ledgers show that rural households of the period lacked the arithmetic they would have needed to reconcile their accounts with neighbors.
Imbalances in Orlen accounts between neighbors, once blamed on poor bookkeeping, may instead have been a deliberate way of keeping households’ relationships open.
Orlen Valley households kept careful accounts with outside merchants because they distrusted those merchants more than they distrusted their own neighbors.
The account between the Brenn and Tamm households shows that disputes between Orlen families were usually caused by the closing of an account.
Parish records demonstrate that whenever an Orlen household repaid a neighbor exactly, a quarrel or lawsuit between the two families soon followed.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle and the old explanation (first paragraph), presents Halvik's alternative (second paragraph), supports it (third and fourth paragraphs), and closes with a hedged 'If Halvik is right'; B captures this, including the hedge. A is the early commentators' view the passage replaces. D is the most tempting trap: the Brenn account is a single illustration and shows a closing coinciding with a quarrel, not causing one, let alone usually. E is too extreme, since the records only 'frequently' note disputes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point of the whole passage: the puzzle, Halvik's answer, and how firmly the author holds it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the imbalances and the 'careless bookkeeping' reading), paragraph 2 (Halvik: the imbalances were deliberate), and the last sentence of paragraph 4 ('If Halvik is right ...').

breakdown.analysis: Structure: a puzzle (neighbors' accounts never balance), an old explanation (sloppy bookkeeping), a new explanation (deliberate, to keep relationships open), evidence, an example, and a hedged wrap-up. Prephrase: the imbalances once blamed on bad bookkeeping may have been a deliberate way to keep households bound. Notice the hedge: the author is sympathetic to Halvik but says 'If Halvik is right,' so the right answer shouldn't declare it proven.

choices.note: That's the early commentators' view, the one the passage sets up to replace.
CORRECT. Puzzle, old explanation, new explanation, and the hedge ('may have been' matches 'If Halvik is right').
The merchant accounts are evidence, not the point, and the passage never says households distrusted merchants. The contrast shows they could balance accounts when they wanted to.

Tempting, because the Brenn account ends with a quarrel. But it's one illustration, it shows the closing and the quarrel in the same year rather than one causing the other, and 'usually' turns one case into a rule.
Too extreme. Paragraph 3 says parish records 'frequently' note a dispute. 'Whenever ... soon followed' adds 'always' and a time order the passage doesn't give.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the accounts that Orlen households kept with grain merchants from outside the valley
choices: were kept less carefully than the households’ accounts with their neighbors
were often left with small remainders whose direction alternated over time
were the only ledger entries that archivists catalogued in the 1950s
were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction with a merchant was complete
frequently gave rise to disputes that were recorded in parish registers
questions.explanation: The second sentence of the third paragraph says the merchant accounts 'were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete,' which is D. B attributes the features of neighbors' accounts to merchants' accounts, and A reverses the contrast the passage draws. E moves the parish-record evidence, which concerns neighbors' accounts closed exactly, onto the merchant accounts. C is never said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage states about the households' accounts with outside grain merchants.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. Paragraph 3 says the same households kept 'precise records' with outside merchants and closed those accounts 'to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete.' Prephrase: merchant accounts were closed exactly. Expect traps that swap features between the two kinds of account.

choices.note: Reversed. The merchant accounts were the precise ones.
These are features of the neighbors' accounts (paragraph 3, 'Nor were the remainders random'). Wrong kind of account.
Never said. The archivists catalogued the account books in general and noticed the neighbors' entries.
CORRECT. Near-verbatim from paragraph 3.
Swaps the evidence. The parish-record disputes go with neighbors' accounts that were closed exactly, not with merchants.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “on the long thread” (last sentence of the second paragraph), the ledgers most probably refer to
choices: a debt that has gone unpaid for so long that the creditor has given up hope of repayment
an account kept open over many years with a grain merchant from outside the valley
an account between neighbors deliberately left unsettled so that the obligation between them continues
a chain of borrowing in which a single loan passed through many households in turn
a record containing errors too numerous for the household’s bookkeeper ever to reconcile
questions.explanation: Halvik cites the expression as the local name for 'such an account,' meaning one in which a small remainder is kept 'perpetually outstanding' to keep the relationship open (second paragraph); that is C. A is tempting because the account is long-lived, but nothing suggests repayment was hoped for and abandoned. B contradicts the third paragraph, where merchant accounts are closed exactly, and E is the early commentators' reading that Halvik rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what kind of account 'on the long thread' names.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 4-5 ('Keeping a small remainder perpetually outstanding ... such an account').

breakdown.analysis: 'Such an account' points back to the previous sentence: one where a small remainder is kept outstanding on purpose to keep the relationship open. So the phrase names a deliberately unsettled account between neighbors. Prephrase: an account left open on purpose to keep two households tied.

choices.note: Tempting, since the thread is 'long.' But the debt isn't abandoned or hopeless; it's kept open on purpose, and it flips back and forth.
Merchant accounts were closed exactly (paragraph 3), so the long-thread phrase can't describe them.
CORRECT. 'Such an account' refers to the deliberately outstanding remainder that keeps the relationship open.
Invented. The passage describes two-household accounts, not a loan passing down a chain.
That's the early commentators' reading, which the expression is cited to undercut.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the interpretation of the ledgers offered by the early commentators depends on
choices: a comparison between the Orlen ledgers and the ledgers kept by households in other valleys during the same period
the belief that a debt left unsettled ended the relationship between the two households involved in it
evidence from parish records that disputes between neighboring households were quite rare during the period
the view that the remainders were too small to have mattered to the households that recorded them
the presumption that the households were trying to make their accounts with neighbors balance
questions.explanation: The commentators read the imbalances as careless bookkeeping or failed arithmetic (first paragraph); that reading treats the ledgers, in the words of the last sentence of the fourth paragraph, as 'failed attempts at reckoning,' so it presumes the households were trying to balance, which is E. B is the tempting reversal: it garbles Halvik's view, on which an exact settlement, not an unsettled debt, ended a relationship. A, C, and D cite comparisons, evidence, and views the passage never attributes to the commentators.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the early commentators' reading (careless bookkeeping, weak arithmetic) has to take for granted.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence (the commentators' reading), and the last sentence of paragraph 4 ('not failed attempts at reckoning').

breakdown.analysis: Ask: you can only call something a mistake if it was trying to be something else. Calling the imbalances careless bookkeeping assumes the households meant to balance the accounts and failed. That's exactly what Halvik denies: the imbalances were the goal. The last sentence makes the contrast explicit: 'not failed attempts at reckoning.' We need an answer saying the commentators presumed the households were aiming at balance.

choices.note: No other valley comes up in connection with the commentators. Invented evidence.
Tempting, because it uses Halvik's vocabulary. But it's backward even as Halvik's view (exact repayment ended relationships), and it isn't something the commentators hold at all.
The passage never says the commentators used parish records, and it doesn't say disputes were rare.
Nothing supports this. Their reading is about the households' failure to reckon, not about whether the remainders mattered.
CORRECT. 'Careless bookkeeping' and 'lacked the arithmetic' only make sense if the goal was balance. That's what the last sentence calls 'failed attempts at reckoning.'

questions.stem: The passage cites each of the following as evidence supporting Halvik’s theory EXCEPT:
choices: testimony from present-day residents of the valley describing a custom of leaving debts unsettled
the exactness with which the same households closed their accounts with grain merchants from outside the valley
the small size of the remainders that were carried forward in accounts between neighboring households
the tendency of the imbalance between two households to alternate, so that each was in turn creditor and debtor
the coincidence of exactly closed accounts between neighbors with disputes, lawsuits, or departures in parish records
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists the evidence: precise merchant accounts (B), small remainders (C), alternating imbalances (D), and parish records linking exact closings to disputes or departures (E). The passage never mentions present-day testimony, so A is the exception. Don't confuse A with the local expression 'on the long thread' (second paragraph), which comes from the ledgers themselves.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Four choices are evidence the passage cites for Halvik; find the one it doesn't cite.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the list of evidence) and paragraph 2, last sentence (the ledger expression).

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice against paragraph 3's list: 1. merchant accounts closed exactly; 2. remainders small; 3. direction alternates; 4. exact closings coincide with disputes, lawsuits, or departures. Anything not on the list is the answer. Watch for a choice that sounds like the 'long thread' expression but changes the source.

choices.note: CORRECT. No present-day residents are mentioned. The 'long thread' expression comes from the ledgers, not from living testimony.
Cited: paragraph 3, second sentence.
Cited: 'they were small, typically less than a tenth of the original loan.'
Cited: 'the direction of the imbalance tended to alternate, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor.'
Cited: the 'Finally' sentence of paragraph 3. It's paraphrased, so it can look unfamiliar, but it's there.

questions.stem: The author discusses the ledger of the Brenn household primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that Orlen households placed a higher value on labor than on grain when settling debts with neighbors
illustrate the kind of arithmetic error that the early commentators attributed to bookkeepers in Orlen households
show in a single case how an alternating imbalance was sustained and how the account was eventually closed
suggest that Halvik’s theory applies more clearly to loans of grain than to loans of labor or tools
establish that quarrels over boundaries were the most common reason that accounts between neighbors came to be closed
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by saying the Brenn ledger 'illustrates the mechanism,' then traces the alternating imbalance for thirty-one years and its closing in the year of a quarrel, which is C. A seizes on one detail (labor valued at slightly more than a bushel) that serves only to show the imbalance flipping. E overgeneralizes from a single case, and B is the commentators' reading the example is meant to replace.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the Brenn example is in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence ('illustrates the mechanism') and the rest of that paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author tells you the job outright: the Brenn ledger 'illustrates the mechanism.' Then it shows the mechanism at work: a remainder flips from one household to the other, the account runs for thirty-one years, and it closes in the year of a quarrel. Prephrase: a worked example of Halvik's mechanism, start to finish.

choices.note: Grabs a detail. Labor valued at a bit more than a bushel just shows how the imbalance flipped; there's no general claim about labor vs. grain.
Opposite purpose. The example shows deliberate imbalance, not the error the commentators assumed.
CORRECT. One account, the alternating imbalance kept going, and the closing at the time of a quarrel.
Nothing suggests the theory fits some kinds of loans better. The Brenn account even mixes grain and labor.
Too broad. One case can't establish what was 'most common,' and the passage doesn't claim it.

questions.stem: If Halvik’s theory is correct, which one of the following would most likely have been true of a household that had newly settled in the Orlen Valley during the period in which the ledgers were kept?
choices: It would have avoided borrowing from its neighbors until it had first established accounts with outside merchants.
To form lasting ties with a neighbor, it would have repaid that neighbor slightly more or less than it had borrowed.
It would have been expected to repay each neighbor exactly until that neighbor had extended it a second loan.
It would have kept its accounts with neighbors in a different unit of measure from the one it used with merchants.
It would have been unable to borrow grain from any neighbor without first performing several days of labor for that neighbor.
questions.explanation: On Halvik's theory, exact repayment signaled a wish to end a relationship and a small outstanding remainder kept it open (second paragraph), so a newcomer seeking ties would leave a remainder, as in B. C is the attractive trap: it invents a probationary custom of exact repayment that, on Halvik's theory, would signal the opposite of what the newcomer wants. A and E have no basis in the passage, and D borrows the idea of measures without support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Halvik's theory to a new case: a household new to the valley.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 3-4 (exact repayment announces an end; a small remainder keeps the relationship open).

breakdown.analysis: Halvik's rule: repay exactly → you're signaling 'we're done.' Leave a small remainder → the relationship stays open. A newcomer who wants to put down roots wants relationships open. So it would repay a little more or a little less. The right answer has to match both parts: the goal (lasting ties) and the means (an inexact repayment).

choices.note: Nothing ties borrowing from neighbors to having merchant accounts first. Invented.
CORRECT. The goal (lasting ties) plus Halvik's means (an inexact repayment that leaves a remainder).
Tempting, because it sounds like a sensible custom for strangers. But under Halvik's theory, repaying exactly would announce that the newcomer didn't want to stay bound. Wrong signal.
The passage never mentions different units of measure for the two kinds of account.
Labor appears only as one way the Brenns repaid a debt. Nothing makes labor a precondition for borrowing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Halvik’s explanation of the imbalances in the Orlen ledgers?
choices: Households in a neighboring valley during the same period kept accounts with their own neighbors that nearly always balanced to the last measure.
The Orlen ledgers rarely record the purposes for which grain, labor, or tools were lent from one household to another.
Several Orlen families whom parish registers record as having quarreled kept carrying small remainders in their accounts with each other.
Households in the valley that kept ledgers tended to be somewhat wealthier than households in the valley that kept no ledgers.
Neighbors, unlike outside merchants, repaid loans in a different local measure from the one borrowed, and the valley’s measures did not convert exactly.
questions.explanation: Halvik says the remainders were deliberate (second paragraph), and her best evidence is that the same households closed merchant accounts exactly and left only small remainders with neighbors (third paragraph). E gives an accidental cause that fits both facts: repayment in a different, inexactly convertible measure, a practice not used with merchants, would leave small remainders with neighbors only. C is the dominant trap. It looks like a counterexample to the parish evidence, but Halvik’s claim runs one way: exact closings often coincided with disputes. She never says a dispute closed the account, so quarreling families who stayed bound fit her view. A concerns another community, and B and D do not bear on why the remainders existed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines Halvik's claim that the imbalances were deliberate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (the theory: remainders kept on purpose) and paragraph 3 (her evidence: exact merchant accounts, small alternating remainders, closings that coincide with disputes).

breakdown.analysis: Halvik's key move is a contrast: the same households were exact with merchants and inexact with neighbors, so the inexactness must be a choice. So what if something mechanical produced exactly that pattern? We want an innocent cause that operates with neighbors and not with merchants. Most students pick (C) because it looks like a counterexample to the quarrel evidence. Read her claim's direction: exact closing → frequently a dispute. (C) gives dispute → no closing. That's the reverse direction, and her theory is fine with it: people can quarrel and still want to stay bound. The right answer doesn't mention deliberateness at all. You have to see that a conversion loss between unequal measures would leave small, never-quite-zero remainders by itself.

choices.note: Another valley could have different customs. A community nearby that balanced its books tells us nothing about why Orlen households didn't.
Irrelevant. Halvik's theory doesn't depend on knowing why things were borrowed.

Tempting. This is the trap: it feels like quarrels don't track closings after all. But Halvik's evidence runs from closing to dispute, not from dispute to closing. Families who quarreled but kept their account open are just people who quarreled and still chose to stay bound. That's consistent with her view.
Irrelevant. Wealth tells us nothing about whether the imbalances were deliberate.

CORRECT. If neighbors (but not merchants) repaid in a different local measure that didn't convert exactly, small remainders would appear with neighbors and not with merchants, with no intention behind them. That supplies an accidental cause for the very contrast Halvik relies on.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Why have courts so seldom exercised their power to appoint expert witnesses of their own choosing?
Should courts make use of their power to appoint expert witnesses of their own choosing?
How can experts retained by the parties be made less partisan in the testimony they give at trial?
What procedures should courts follow in selecting the experts whom they appoint in technical disputes?
Are jurors capable of choosing rationally between the conflicting conclusions of two partisan experts?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that judges are right to be reluctant to appoint their own experts, and passage B argues for appointing them; both are centrally about whether courts should use the power, which is B. A is the closest trap: passage A explains judges' reluctance in its first paragraph, but passage B never asks why the power is seldom used. D is a concern of passage B's third paragraph only, E of passage B's first paragraph only, and C is touched only by passage A's closing remedy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one question that both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1 ('sound reasons for the reluctance') and paragraph 4 (the alternative remedy); passage B, paragraph 2 (the case for a court-appointed expert).

breakdown.analysis: A says: don't use the power, here's why. B says: use it, here's why and how. Same question, opposite answers: should courts appoint their own experts? Every 'both' answer must be central to A and to B. Watch for questions only one passage takes up.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage A opens with the power being 'seldom used.' But A's concern is whether the reluctance is justified, and B never discusses why courts seldom use the power. Only one passage, and not even A's main concern.
CORRECT. A answers no, B answers yes. That's the shared question.
Only passage A's last sentence gestures at improving adversarial testing, and it doesn't try to make party experts less partisan. B accepts party experts as partisan and looks elsewhere.
Selection procedures are passage B's third paragraph only. A raises selection as a problem, not as a procedure to design.
Passage B's first paragraph worries about this. Passage A never addresses jurors' ability to choose between party experts.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B?
choices: the possibility that a judge could ask a professional body to propose candidates for appointment
the existence of technical fields in which competent specialists disagree with one another
the tendency of jurors to credit whichever of two experts seems more poised and likable
the reluctance of attorneys to cross-examine forcefully an expert witness whom the judge has chosen
the right of parties to present their own experts even when the court has appointed one
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph of passage A says a lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge's witness 'risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk'; passage B says only that parties 'remain free' to cross-examine the court's expert, which is about permission, not reluctance, so D is correct. B is the likeliest trap, but it appears in both passages (A's 'competent specialists disagree,' third paragraph; B's 'Where a field is genuinely divided,' third paragraph). A, C, and E appear only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the item that passage A mentions and passage B does not.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 4 (lawyers' reluctance to cross-examine the court's expert) and paragraph 3 (divided fields); passage B, paragraphs 1-3.

breakdown.analysis: Two checks per choice: is it in A? Is it absent from B? Lawyers being reluctant to go hard at the judge's own witness is A's third objection (its fourth paragraph). B mentions cross-examining the court's expert only to say the parties 'remain free' to do it. Free to do it isn't the same as reluctant to do it.

choices.note: Only in passage B (third paragraph: 'ask a professional body to propose a panel').
Tempting, because it's prominent in A's 'Second' paragraph. But B mentions it too: 'Where a field is genuinely divided.' In both, so it fails.
Only in passage B (first paragraph, the mock-juror studies).
CORRECT. Passage A's fourth paragraph: 'few lawyers will run that risk.' B talks only about the parties' freedom to cross-examine, not any reluctance.
Only in passage B (second paragraph: 'The parties remain free to call their own witnesses').

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that some experts retained by litigants are too
choices: accommodating
cautious
specialized
numerous
inexpensive
questions.explanation: The second sentence of passage B says litigants retain the expert whose views 'for an adequate fee, can be made to serve' their case, implying that some experts are too willing to shape their views to suit whoever pays them: too accommodating (A). E inverts the reference to fees, which concerns experts' willingness to be paid for favorable views, not their cost. B, C, and D have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the word for what passage B implies is wrong with some party experts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, second sentence ('for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it').

breakdown.analysis: 'Whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it.' Translation: pay them and they'll say what you need. So they bend too easily to the client. Prephrase: too pliable, too willing to please.

choices.note: CORRECT. Views that can be 'made to serve' a case for a fee are too accommodating.
Opposite of B's picture. The experts are 'confident,' and they bend toward the client rather than hedging.
No support. Nothing says party experts are too narrow in their fields.
B says litigants interview 'several,' but never says there are too many experts.
Tempting only if you misread 'an adequate fee.' The point is that experts can be paid to shift their views, not that they're cheap.

questions.stem: The relationship between passage A and passage B is most analogous to the relationship between the documents described in which one of the following?
choices: an essay titled “Why Arbitrators Should Rely on the Parties’ Rival Appraisals” and an essay titled “Improving the Exchange of Appraisal Reports Before Hearings”
an essay titled “In Defense of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “The Dangers of Letting Arbitrators Choose Their Own Appraisers”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “How Parties to Arbitration Can Choose Better Appraisers of Their Own”
an essay titled “A Short History of Appraisal in Arbitration” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
questions.explanation: Passage A criticizes a decision maker's appointing its own supposedly neutral expert, and passage B defends that practice as giving decision makers a fixed point between rival partisan experts (second paragraph of passage B); E reproduces both stances, in order, and B's 'fixed point' rationale. B reverses the order of the two stances. C is the closest trap: its first title matches passage A, but its second is about improving the parties' own experts, not defending the decision maker's expert. A has two essays favoring the adversarial approach, and D's first essay is historical rather than critical.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the pair of titles whose relationship mirrors A (against court-chosen experts) then B (for them).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1 (the stance) and paragraphs 2-4 (the objections); passage B, paragraph 2 ('a fixed point against which to measure them').

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the courtroom: essay 1 attacks a decision maker hiring its own 'neutral' expert; essay 2 defends it because it gives a benchmark between two hired guns. Order matters: critique first, defense second. Check each pair for both halves and for the order.

choices.note: Both titles favor relying on the parties' own experts, which is A's side only. No defense of the arbitrator's expert.
Right two stances, wrong order. Defense first, critique second is B-then-A.
Tempting: the first title is a perfect match for passage A. But the second is about parties choosing better experts of their own, not a defense of the arbitrator's expert.
The first essay is a neutral history, but passage A is a critique.
CORRECT. A critique of the decision maker's own appraiser, then a defense built on the 'benchmark between rival valuations' idea, which matches B's 'fixed point.'

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: jurors are likely to give a court-appointed expert’s testimony more weight than they give the testimony of either party’s expert
parties should be permitted to cross-examine an expert whom the court itself has appointed
jurors’ readiness to defer to an expert chosen by the court counts against the practice of appointing one
the testimony of experts retained by litigants tends to reflect the interests of the litigants who retained them
competent specialists in some technical fields sometimes reach conflicting conclusions on questions that come before a court
questions.explanation: Passage A’s first objection (second paragraph) is that jurors will treat the court’s expert’s opinion ‘as a verdict to be ratified’; passage B replies (second paragraph) that if jurors give that expert more weight, ‘that is hardly a defect.’ So they disagree over whether jurors’ deference counts against appointment, which is C. A is the dominant trap: passage A asserts that jurors will give the court’s expert more weight, but passage B never denies it; its ‘if’ clause leaves the point open. D and E are views both authors hold, and B is something passage A never addresses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would accept and the other would reject. Both authors must take a side.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 2 (jurors treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'); passage B paragraph 2 ('if jurors give the court's expert more weight ... that is hardly a defect').

breakdown.analysis: Do the authors disagree about whether jurors defer to the court's expert, or about whether that deference is bad? Look at B's wording: 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight.' That's an 'if'. B never says they won't. So the disagreement isn't about the fact; it's about what the fact means. A says it's a reason against appointment. B says it's no defect. We need an answer about the significance of the deference. Most students pick (A) because it's the most obvious point of contrast. But to disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Passage B never says no.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. Passage A says yes. But passage B says only 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight', which is a conditional, not a denial. B has no stated view on whether they will, so there's no disagreement here.
Passage B says the parties remain free to cross-examine. Passage A never says they shouldn't be; it says lawyers are reluctant to do it hard. No disagreement.

CORRECT. A treats jurors' deference as a reason not to appoint (the expert 'effectively' decides the case). B says the extra weight is 'hardly a defect'. One yes, one no, on whether the deference counts against the practice.
Both agree. A calls for a remedy for 'partisan expertise'; B says litigants pick experts whose views serve their case.
Both agree. A says competent specialists disagree in unsettled fields; B's 'two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable' and its 'range of respectable opinion' concede the same.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in the last sentence of passage B?
choices: Such an instruction would discourage jurors from giving the court’s expert the additional weight that the expert’s neutrality rightly warrants.
Jurors who know that the judge chose the expert will likely go on treating that expert’s opinion as authoritative.
Such an instruction would reveal to jurors a fact about how the expert was selected that they would otherwise never learn.
Such an instruction would make attorneys more willing to cross-examine the court’s expert aggressively, needlessly prolonging technical trials.
Such an instruction would be unnecessary, since jurors already regard the court’s expert as no more reliable than other witnesses.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of passage B proposes telling jurors that the court's expert is a witness like any other. Passage A's first objection (second paragraph) is that jurors told a witness was chosen by the judge treat that witness's opinion 'not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified'; an instruction that leaves jurors knowing who chose the expert would not dispel that aura, so B is correct. A states passage B's view of the added weight, not passage A's. C is tempting because passage A says the jury 'will never learn' something, but that refers to the choice of doctrine (third paragraph). D and E conflict with passage A's own concerns.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how A's author would object to B's proposal that judges tell jurors the court's expert is 'a witness like any other.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 3, last sentence (the jury instruction); passage A, paragraph 2 (jurors treat the court's witness as authoritative).

breakdown.analysis: First find the suggestion: the last sentence of B, a jury instruction that the court's expert is just another witness. Now think like A. A's first worry is that jurors who know the judge picked the expert defer to that expert. Would a sentence from the judge undo that? A would doubt it: the jurors still know who chose the witness. Prephrase: the instruction won't stop the deference.

choices.note: That's B's view (the court's expert 'deserves more weight'), not A's. A thinks the extra weight is the problem.
CORRECT. A's second paragraph says knowing the judge chose the witness turns opinion into 'a verdict to be ratified.' An instruction doesn't erase that knowledge.

Tempting, because A says the jury 'will never learn' something. But that's about the hidden choice of doctrine in a divided field (A's third paragraph), not about who selected the expert. Jurors already know that.
Backward. A worries lawyers won't cross-examine the court's expert; it wouldn't complain that they'd do it more.
Contradicts A, which says jurors see the court's expert as more neutral than any party's expert.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the remedy proposed in the last sentence of passage A as inadequate on the grounds that it
choices: would deprive the parties of the opportunity to cross-examine opposing experts in the presence of the jury
would still leave a judge who lacks the relevant expertise to determine which of two conflicting experts is correct
would require jurors to master the technical reasoning that the opposing experts present at pretrial hearings
would give jurors no reference point beyond the parties’ own witnesses for judging between two conflicting expert opinions at trial
would make litigants’ selection of experts whose views serve their case even more strategic than it already is
questions.explanation: Passage B locates the problem in jurors having ‘no basis for choosing between’ two partisan experts (first paragraph) and offers the court’s expert as ‘a fixed point against which to measure them’ (second paragraph). Passage A’s remedy, earlier disclosure and pretrial confrontation between the parties’ experts, still leaves jurors with only partisan experts to compare, so D is correct. B is the dominant trap: a judge lacking expertise is passage A’s worry about selection, and passage A’s remedy gives the judge no role in deciding which expert is right. Passage B’s complaint is about jurors. C puts jurors at pretrial hearings, and A and E have no basis in either passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why passage B's author would find passage A's fix (more disclosure, pretrial confrontation of experts) not good enough.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of passage A (the remedy); passage B paragraph 1 (jurors have 'no basis for choosing') and paragraph 2 (the court's expert as 'a fixed point').

breakdown.analysis: What is B's problem with partisan experts, exactly? Not that the experts are biased as such. It's that jurors facing two irreconcilable experts have nothing to measure them by, so they go with the more likable one. Does A's remedy fix that? Earlier reports and pretrial hearings sharpen the parties' experts, but at trial jurors still face two partisan witnesses and no neutral benchmark. We need an answer that says: jurors still lack an independent yardstick. Most students pick (B) because 'a judge who lacks the relevant expertise' is a phrase they remember from the comparative set. But that worry belongs to passage A, it concerns choosing an expert, and A's remedy doesn't ask the judge to pick a winner at all.

choices.note: Nothing in A's remedy removes cross-examination. Pretrial confrontation adds testing; it doesn't take any away.

Tempting. This is the trap. The judge-lacks-expertise idea comes from passage A's second objection, about choosing an expert. Passage A's remedy involves no judicial choice of expert and no judge deciding who is right, and passage B's complaint is about what jurors lack.
The jury isn't at pretrial hearings. Nothing in either passage says the remedy asks jurors to master anything new.

CORRECT. B's whole case is that jurors need 'a fixed point' against which to measure the parties' experts. A's remedy improves the parties' experts but leaves jurors with only those experts to compare.
Neither passage suggests disclosure or pretrial hearings would make expert shopping worse. Pure invention.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: describe how a hypothesis about a species’ decline was proposed, disputed, and largely borne out
explain why a regional cleanup program failed to improve water quality in a river above a dam
argue that funds for protecting freshwater mussels should go to fish passage rather than water quality
compare the laboratory methods used to study mussel larvae with the field methods used to age adult mussels
show that critics of a biologist’s account of a species’ decline were mistaken in every respect
questions.explanation: The passage presents a puzzle (first paragraph), Kovač's hypothesis (second paragraph), objections to it (third paragraph), and later evidence that largely confirmed it while crediting one objection (fourth paragraph), which is A. C is the trap: it is Kovač's recommendation (third paragraph), not the author's purpose. B contradicts the first paragraph, where water quality met every standard; D seizes on two methods; and E is contradicted by the concession that the critics identified 'a real, though secondary, constraint.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State why the author wrote the passage as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs: decline and failed cleanup (1), Kovač's hypothesis (2), resistance (3), the fish lift's results (4).

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. mussels kept declining after the water was cleaned; 2. Kovač: it's the missing host fish, blocked by the dam; 3. critics push back (lab vs. river; sediment); 4. a fish lift brings the herring back, juveniles appear, and the critics turn out partly right. Prephrase: to tell how a hypothesis was proposed, challenged, and mostly confirmed. The author narrates; the author doesn't campaign.

choices.note: CORRECT. Proposed (paragraph 2), disputed (paragraph 3), largely borne out (paragraph 4). 'Largely' leaves room for the critics' secondary point.
Contradicts paragraph 1: water quality met every standard by the late 1980s. The cleanup worked on the water; the mussels kept declining anyway.
Tempting, because Kovač 'urged' this. But that's one person's recommendation in paragraph 3, not the passage's purpose.
The passage mentions both methods, but it never compares them. Detail, not purpose.
Too strong. Paragraph 4 credits the critics with 'a real, though secondary, constraint.'

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: How many weeks do slate pearlmussel glochidia remain encapsulated on a Halder herring before they drop off as juveniles?
Which fish species other than the Halder herring did Kovač expose to glochidia in her laboratory tests?
How much did the fish lift at the Ostrow Dam cost to build, and who paid for its operation?
Why do slate pearlmussels live longer than most other freshwater mussel species found in the Halder River?
Why did the improvement in water quality above the Ostrow Dam fail to halt the mussels’ decline there?
questions.explanation: The passage explains that the dam ended the herring runs on which glochidia depend, so the upstream population could not reproduce whatever the water quality (second paragraph), answering E. A is the tempting trap, but the passage says only 'several weeks,' not a number. B, C, and D ask for information the passage never gives; it says adults live long, but not why, or how that compares with other mussels.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (water quality met every standard; the mussels kept declining) and paragraph 2 (glochidia need the herring; the dam ended its runs).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; test each question against the passage. The passage's whole story answers one question: why didn't cleaning up the water save the mussels? Because their larvae need the herring, and the dam kept the herring out. Watch for questions that sound answered because the topic is mentioned but the specific fact (a number, a list, a reason) isn't given.

choices.note: Tempting, since the passage covers this stage. But it says only 'several weeks.' No number, so no answer.
The passage says Kovač tested 'a dozen fish species' but never names them.
Cost and funding of the lift are never mentioned.
The passage says adults live 'for most of a century,' but never explains why or compares them with other species.
CORRECT. Paragraphs 1-2: the decline came from the loss of the host fish blocked by the dam, not from the water, so cleaner water couldn't stop it.

questions.stem: The author mentions that recruitment was markedly lower in the siltiest reaches (third sentence of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the fish lift has so far failed to restore reproduction in most of the river above the dam
show that Kovač’s critics were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive above the dam
concede that an objection to Kovač’s account identified a real factor, though not the main one
argue that funding for measures to reduce sediment and pollution above the dam should now be restored
cast doubt on Kovač’s laboratory findings about which fish species could serve as hosts for glochidia
questions.explanation: The sentence concedes that the sediment critics 'had identified a real, though secondary, constraint,' after the previous sentence has shown juveniles appearing even where sediment had not changed; that is C. B is the trap: it takes the concession too far, since recruitment resumed once herring returned, showing that host absence, not sediment, explained the missing age classes. A exaggerates 'lower' into failure, and D and E are not suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the sentence about lower recruitment in silty reaches does in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2-3 (juveniles found even where sediment had not changed; 'a real, though secondary, constraint'); paragraph 3 (the sediment objection).

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before it: juveniles came back above the dam, even in reaches where sediment hadn't changed. That's a win for Kovač. Then: 'nonetheless' recruitment was lower in the siltiest reaches, so the sediment critics were onto something real, just not the main cause. Prephrase: a partial concession to the critics.

choices.note: Exaggerates. 'Markedly lower' in the siltiest reaches isn't failure in most of the river; juveniles were recovered above the dam.

Tempting, because it's about the same critics. But the critics claimed sediment explained the missing age classes. The return of juveniles once herring returned shows it didn't; sediment was 'secondary.'
CORRECT. 'A real, though secondary, constraint' is a concession that the objection was partly right.
The passage recommends no funding change in paragraph 4. It reports results.
The sentence concerns sediment, not hosts. And herring carrying glochidia upstream supports Kovač's host findings.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the conclusions Kovač drew in 1994?
choices: Adult slate pearlmussels upstream of the dam grow more slowly than those downstream, so their growth rings are harder to count.
Glochidia of several other mussel species in the Halder River transform successfully on many different species of fish.
Halder herring tolerate polluted water better than most other fish species that once inhabited the river do.
Pearlmussels in a sediment-free tributary entering the Halder above the dam are likewise nearly all over sixty-five years old.
Juvenile mussels of many species prove to be even more sensitive to fine sediment than biologists believed in 1994.
questions.explanation: Kovač's critics proposed sediment above the dam as an alternative explanation for the missing age classes (third paragraph); D shows the same age gap where there is no sediment but the herring are still blocked, ruling out that alternative. E strengthens the critics rather than Kovač, and A casts doubt on her aging method. B concerns other species, and C is irrelevant to whether the herring's absence prevents reproduction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most supports Kovač's claim that the upstream mussels stopped reproducing because the dam cut off their host fish.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Kovač's findings and conclusion) and paragraph 3 (the sediment objection).

breakdown.analysis: Kovač: no herring → no juveniles. Critics: maybe it's the sediment above the dam killing juveniles. To strengthen Kovač, rule out the rival cause.
