Find a place above the dam (no herring) without sediment. If young mussels are still missing there, sediment can't be the reason. We want an answer that holds herring access fixed and removes sediment.

choices.note: Weakens, if anything: harder-to-count rings cast doubt on the ages Kovač relied on.
Other species aren't the issue. That they use many hosts says nothing about whether the slate pearlmussel needs the herring.
Irrelevant. Herring's tolerance for pollution doesn't bear on whether its absence explains the missing juveniles.
CORRECT. Above the dam (no herring) but sediment-free, and still no young mussels. That rules out the critics' sediment explanation.
Tempting, since it's about juveniles. But it helps the critics' sediment explanation, not Kovač's.

questions.stem: The information yielded by which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether the critics described in the third paragraph were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive?
choices: placing adult pearlmussels taken from below the dam in cages on the riverbed above the dam and monitoring their survival
caging hatchery-raised juvenile pearlmussels on the riverbed above the dam and comparing their survival there with survival below it
comparing the number of glochidia released by female pearlmussels above the dam with the number released by females below it
counting the growth rings of slate pearlmussels collected from several sites on the river below the dam
exposing slate pearlmussel glochidia in the laboratory to additional fish species that are found above the dam
questions.explanation: The sediment critics (third paragraph) claimed the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive, not whether they were produced. B supplies juveniles directly and tests their survival in the upstream riverbed against a downstream baseline, separating survival from production. A is the dominant trap: it runs the right kind of caged-survival test on the wrong animals. The passage says juveniles are more sensitive to sediment than adults, so adult survival says little about whether juveniles could live there. C bears on larval output, E tests the other objection (hosts in the wild), and D looks only below the dam.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the experiment whose result would tell you whether the sediment critics were right: were juveniles missing above the dam because they couldn't survive there?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last three sentences (fine sediment above the dam; juveniles 'more sensitive to such sediment than adults are'; the missing age classes 'might reflect where juveniles could survive').

breakdown.analysis: The critics split two questions: were juveniles being produced, and could they survive? To test survival, you have to take production out of the picture: put juveniles there yourself and see if they live. A comparison with juveniles below the dam tells you whether the upstream bed is the problem. Most students pick (A) because it has the right design: cages on the upstream riverbed, track survival. But read who goes in the cage. Adults. The critics' claim was about juveniles, and the passage says juveniles are more sensitive than adults. Adults thriving up there proves nothing. One word decides this question.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. Right design, wrong animal. The passage says juveniles are 'more sensitive to such sediment than adults are', so adults surviving above the dam wouldn't show that juveniles could.
CORRECT. Putting juveniles on the upstream riverbed removes the question of production and isolates survival; the downstream comparison shows whether the upstream bed is what kills them.
This measures larval output, which bears on production, the very thing the critics said might not be the issue.
Below the dam isn't where the age classes are missing. This tells you nothing about the upstream bed.
This tests the other objection (wild hosts that fare poorly in tanks), not the sediment claim.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the surveys of the 1970s mentioned in the first paragraph?
choices: They used methods unable to detect juvenile mussels burrowed in the riverbed and so missed young mussels that were present.
Their findings were inconsistent with the view that industrial pollution and sediment were responsible for the decline.
They should have led biologists to examine the mussel’s life cycle rather than the condition of the river’s water.
The decline they recorded would not by itself have revealed that the population above the dam had ceased to reproduce.
They counted mussels below the dam as well as above it, which obscured the difference between the two populations.
questions.explanation: The surveys recorded falling numbers. Kovač’s insight required aging the mussels, because a population of long-lived adults that has stopped reproducing appears ‘merely diminished’ (second paragraph) and ‘can conceal a failure of reproduction’ (last paragraph), which supports D. A is the dominant trap: it borrows a real fact (juveniles burrow in the riverbed, third paragraph) to invent a flaw in the survey methods that the passage never describes, and Kovač’s aging found that young mussels upstream really were missing. B fails because a decline in numbers fits a pollution explanation, which is why that explanation was accepted; C imports a judgment the author never makes; E contradicts the first paragraph, which places the surveys upstream.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage supports about the 1970s surveys: what they could and couldn't show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the surveys upstream found fewer mussels each decade); paragraph 2, last two sentences (aging the mussels; 'reproductively dead ... while appearing merely diminished'); last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: What did the surveys actually measure? Numbers. And what was really going on? No reproduction, hidden by long-lived adults. So could a falling count, by itself, tell you reproduction had stopped? No: a dying-but-not-reproducing population and a population thinned by pollution both just look smaller. That's what the right answer has to say, and it says it in a weak, hedged way ('would not by itself have revealed'). Most students pick (A) because it sounds like the scientific explanation of what went wrong, and it uses a real fact: juveniles burrow. But the passage never says how the surveys were run, and Kovač's aging confirmed that young mussels upstream were actually missing, not hidden. Hard RC traps often stitch a passage fact onto a claim the passage never makes.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. Juveniles do burrow (paragraph 3), but the passage says nothing about survey methods, and Kovač found that nearly all upstream mussels really were over sixty-five. The young ones weren't hiding; they weren't there.
A decline fits a pollution explanation perfectly well, which is why that explanation was accepted. The problem came when the decline continued after the cleanup, decades later.
A normative judgment the author never makes. The author says the episode is a caution, not that the 1970s surveyors should have looked elsewhere.

CORRECT. Counts can't separate 'diminished' from 'reproductively dead' in a long-lived species; it took aging the mussels. The passage's 'appearing merely diminished' and 'can conceal a failure of reproduction' say exactly this.
Contradicted. Paragraph 1 says the surveys were 'upstream of the Ostrow Dam'.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Our league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game. The rule's supporters say it will reduce arm injuries, and that is a worthy aim. But most arm injuries among our players occur during off-season travel tournaments, which the league does not govern. So a pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the coach's argument?
choices: Reducing arm injuries among the league's youth pitchers is a worthy aim that the rule's supporters share.
A limit on pitches in league games would do little to protect the arms of the league's young players.
Most arm injuries suffered by the league's players occur during off-season travel tournaments.
The league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game.
The league should begin to govern the off-season travel tournaments in which most arm injuries occur.
questions.explanation: The coach's point is the opening claim that the league should not adopt the pitch limit; everything else supports it, so D is correct. B is the trap: it is supported by the claim about travel tournaments, but it is offered as the reason for rejecting the rule, so it is an intermediate conclusion. C is a premise, A a concession, and E is never proposed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The league should not adopt the forty-pitch limit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reducing arm injuries is worthy (concession); but most arm injuries happen in off-season travel tournaments the league doesn't govern; so a league pitch limit would do little to protect arms.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Here it comes first, which is common. The "So" sentence at the end looks like a conclusion, but ask why the coach says it: to explain why the league shouldn't adopt the rule. That makes it a stepping stone. Lesson: "so" doesn't always mark the main conclusion.

choices.note: A concession. The coach grants that the aim is worthy before arguing against the rule. Not the point being proved.
Tempting. It's flagged by "So" and it is supported by the tournament fact. But it's offered as the reason not to adopt the rule. Intermediate, not main.
A premise. It's the evidence that a league pitch limit wouldn't help much.
CORRECT. The opening claim. The travel-tournament fact and the little protection the rule would give are both there to support it.
The coach never proposes this. Saying the league doesn't govern tournaments isn't saying it should.

questions.stimulus: Kessel's Bakery began setting out free samples of its pastries on the front counter at the start of March. The bakery's pastry sales in March were 15 percent higher than its pastry sales in February. Clearly, offering free samples is an effective way for the bakery to increase its pastry sales, and it should continue the practice.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that customers who tried a sample bought only the kind of pastry they had sampled
fails to establish that the increase in pastry sales led to any increase in the bakery's overall profits for March
overlooks the possibility that some factor other than the samples accounts for the rise in March pastry sales
takes for granted that a practice that works for one bakery will work equally well for every other bakery
treats a single month's increase in sales as proof that sales will keep rising at that rate every month
questions.explanation: The argument infers that the samples caused the March increase merely because the increase followed them; a seasonal change or some other factor could explain it, so C is correct. B is tempting, but the conclusion is about increasing pastry sales, not profits. The argument never generalizes to other bakeries (D), never predicts a continuing rate of growth (E), and needs nothing about which pastries were bought (A).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Free samples are an effective way to increase the bakery's pastry sales, so the bakery should keep offering them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Samples started in March; March pastry sales were 15 percent above February's.

breakdown.analysis: So sales went up after the samples appeared. Does that mean the samples did it? March might just be a better month for pastries than February, or the bakery might have changed something else. This is the classic before-and-after causal flaw: X came before Y, so X caused Y. We need an answer that says the argument ignores other possible causes of the rise.

choices.note: We don't know this, and the argument doesn't need it. Sales of any pastry count, whether or not it was the one sampled.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone who tasted our lemon tart bought something, so the tart sample must be what they bought.

choices.note: Tempting, because a business owner would care about profit. But the conclusion is only that samples increase pastry sales. The LSAT is ultra specific: sales, not profit.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our sales rose 10 percent, so the business is now more profitable (ignoring that costs rose 20 percent).

choices.note: CORRECT. The only evidence is that sales rose after the samples began. Season, weather, a new product or a nearby event could explain the rise just as well.
The argument never talks about other bakeries. Its conclusion is about this bakery only.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Samples raised sales at Kessel's, so they will raise sales at every bakery in town.

choices.note: The argument claims the samples are effective, not that sales will keep climbing 15 percent a month. Nothing in it is about future rates.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Sales rose 15 percent in March, so they will rise 15 percent every month this year.

questions.stimulus: Striped grunters, a reef fish common off Varrow Island, feed mostly at night, which is when they are most active. Yet in the island's annual reef census, conducted each spring by volunteers, divers who survey the reef during the day consistently count far more striped grunters than do divers who survey the same stretches of reef at night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why divers count more striped grunters by day than by night?
choices: Several species of eels that prey on striped grunters hunt over the reef mainly at night, when the grunters are active.
At night striped grunters leave the reef to feed in distant seagrass beds, returning to rest over the reef by day.
Divers who survey the reef at night carry powerful lights that make fish visible from a considerable distance.
The striped grunter is among the most numerous of all the fish species that live on the reef around Varrow Island.
Many of the other fish species found in the waters near Varrow Island also do most of their feeding at night.
questions.explanation: You would expect a fish active at night to be easier to find at night. B explains the pattern: the grunters feed away from the reef at night and are over the reef, where divers survey, by day. C deepens the puzzle, A does not explain why the fish would be seen more often by day, and D and E do not distinguish day from night counts.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Striped grunters are most active at night, but divers count far more of them on the reef by day.

breakdown.analysis: Why would an active fish be harder to find? Activity isn't the same as being where the divers look. We need an answer that puts the grunters somewhere other than the surveyed reef at night, or makes them harder to see then.

choices.note: Predators hunting at night might make grunters hide, but the answer doesn't say that. Eels hunting at night don't by themselves explain why divers see fewer grunters on the reef.
CORRECT. Divers survey the reef. At night the grunters are off in the seagrass beds; by day they're resting right over the reef. So more are counted by day.
Wrong direction. Powerful lights should make night counts higher, which deepens the puzzle.
Interesting fact, but it applies day and night alike. Abundance can't explain a difference between the two.
So? Other species' habits say nothing about why grunter counts differ between day and night.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The Marlton city orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works. Those works draw the largest audiences, and ticket sales are what keep the orchestra solvent.

Malik: Ticket sales certainly matter. But an orchestra that plays only familiar works will gradually lose younger listeners, who are its future audience. The orchestra should give a substantial share of its programs to new compositions.
questions.stem: Rosa and Malik disagree over whether
choices: the orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works
established classical works draw larger audiences than new compositions do at the orchestra's concerts
younger listeners generally prefer new compositions to the established classical works the orchestra now plays
ticket sales are important to the overall financial health of the Marlton city orchestra
the orchestra is currently at risk of becoming insolvent because of declining ticket sales
questions.explanation: Rosa says nearly all programs should be established works; Malik says a substantial share should go to new compositions, which rules out 'nearly all,' so they disagree about A. Malik concedes that ticket sales matter (D) and never disputes that classics draw larger audiences (B). Rosa says nothing about younger listeners (C), and neither says the orchestra is at risk (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rosa: nearly all programs should be established classics, because they draw the biggest audiences and ticket sales keep the orchestra solvent; Malik: ticket sales matter, but playing only familiar works loses younger listeners, so a substantial share of programs should be new works.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Rosa's yes: nearly all programs should be classics. Malik's no: a substantial share should be new compositions, which can't happen if nearly all are classics. Watch for answers where only one of them takes a side.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rosa says yes outright. Malik's "substantial share" for new works means no.
Rosa says this, but Malik never denies it. He argues about the future audience, not current draws.
Tempting, because Malik talks about younger listeners. But he says they'd drift away from familiar works, and Rosa says nothing about them at all. Only one side takes a position.
Malik agrees: "Ticket sales certainly matter." An agreement point, not a disagreement.
Neither speaker says the orchestra is in trouble now. Rosa only says ticket sales keep it solvent.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: This summer the tomato plants I mulched with straw produced far fewer split fruits than the unmulched tomato plants in my neighbor's plot did, although we set out our seedlings on the same day. Tomatoes split when soil moisture swings sharply, and a layer of straw keeps soil moisture steady. So mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gardener's argument?
choices: The few unmulched tomato plants in the gardener's own plot split about as often as the neighbor's plants did.
Some tomato varieties are much more prone to splitting than others, whatever the moisture of the soil they grow in.
The gardener's neighbor harvested more tomatoes in total this summer than the gardener did, despite using no mulch.
Straw mulch also suppresses weeds that compete with tomato plants for water and nutrients in the soil.
Tomato splitting tends to be more widespread in summers with heavy rain late in the growing season.
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two different plots, so a difference other than mulch (variety, soil, watering) could explain the result. A shows that unmulched plants in the gardener's own plot split as often as the neighbor's, isolating the mulch as the difference. B raises a possible alternative cause and so, if anything, weakens; E would affect both plots alike; C and D are off the point.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The gardener's mulched plants split far less than the neighbor's unmulched plants; splitting comes from moisture swings, and straw steadies moisture.

breakdown.analysis: So the gardener's plot did better. Was it the straw, or the plot? Different gardens can differ in soil, variety, watering and shade. We need an answer that rules out the plot difference, ideally by comparing mulched and unmulched plants under the same conditions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same plot, same gardener, no mulch: these plants split like the neighbor's. So the plot itself isn't what protected the mulched plants; the mulch is.
Tempting, because variety does matter. But it points to an alternative cause, which hurts the argument rather than helping it.
Total harvest isn't splitting. Interesting fact, but not relevant.
A second benefit of mulch, but the argument is about splitting, not weeds.
Rain would hit both plots the same way. It doesn't explain the difference or tie it to mulch.

questions.stimulus: Last year the city raised the fare on its Route 9 buses from $1.50 to $2.00, and since then ridership on Route 9 has fallen by about a third. The city's transit planners have concluded that if the fare is returned to $1.50, most of the riders that Route 9 has lost will come back to it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the planners' argument?
choices: Ridership on several of the city's other bus routes, whose fares were also raised last year, fell as well.
Even at $2.00, the Route 9 fare remains lower than the bus fares charged in most comparable cities.
Returning the Route 9 fare to $1.50 would reduce the revenue that the transit system collects from each rider.
Some regular Route 9 riders have complained to the city about crowded buses during the morning rush hour.
Soon after the fare rose, a new light-rail line opened along most of Route 9, drawing many of its riders.
questions.explanation: The planners assume the fare increase drove riders away, so cutting the fare would bring them back. E gives another cause of the decline, a competing rail line, which a fare cut would not undo. A tends to support the fare explanation, B compares cities rather than explaining the decline, C concerns revenue, and D is too small a complaint to matter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Returning the fare to $1.50 will bring most of the lost Route 9 riders back.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ridership fell by a third after the fare went from $1.50 to $2.00.

breakdown.analysis: Riders left after the fare rose. Did they leave because the fare rose? Something else might have happened at the same time. We need another reason riders left, one that a lower fare wouldn't fix.

choices.note: Wrong direction. If ridership fell wherever fares rose, that points to the fare as the cause, which helps the planners.
So? Being cheap compared with other cities doesn't mean riders here didn't react to the increase.
Revenue is a different issue. The argument is about whether riders return, not whether the city can afford it.
A few complaints about crowding don't explain a one-third drop, and crowding would ease as riders leave anyway.
CORRECT. Many riders left for the new rail line. Lowering the bus fare won't undo that, so the planners' cause-and-cure story falls apart.

questions.stimulus: In Darrow County, defendants awaiting trial who cannot afford bail remain in jail. A study of the county's criminal cases found that defendants held in jail before trial were more likely to plead guilty than were released defendants facing similar charges and comparably strong evidence. Many of the jailed defendants who pleaded guilty were sentenced to the time they had already served.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the defendants in Darrow County who plead guilty to the charges against them are in fact innocent.
Defendants in Darrow County who are released before trial are less likely than jailed defendants to be convicted at trial.
Some defendants' choices about whether to plead guilty are partly influenced by factors other than the evidence against them.
Bail amounts set in Darrow County are higher, on average, than those set in most other counties in the state.
Eliminating bail in Darrow County would reduce the number of guilty pleas entered there by roughly half.
questions.explanation: Jailed and released defendants with comparably strong evidence pleaded guilty at different rates, so something besides the evidence, such as being jailed, affects some decisions to plead; C follows. A is the tempting overreach: the facts show pleas are influenced by detention, not that most who plead are innocent. B, D, and E bring in trials, other counties, and a specific number the facts do not address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Defendants who can't afford bail stay in jail before trial; 2. jailed defendants pleaded guilty more often than released defendants with similar charges and similar evidence; 3. many jailed defendants who pleaded guilty got time served.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase exactly, but fact 2 is the key. Same charges, same strength of evidence, different plea rates. So the evidence can't be the whole story. Watch for answers that exaggerate that into claims about innocence or exact numbers.

choices.note: Too strong. Being influenced by detention doesn't mean most people who plead are innocent. Many may be guilty and just want out.
We don't know this. The study is about pleas, not trial outcomes.
CORRECT. Evidence was held comparable, yet jailed defendants pleaded more often. So for some defendants something besides the evidence, like being in jail, shapes the decision. 'Some' keeps it safe.
No other counties are mentioned. We can't rank Darrow's bail amounts.
Too specific. Nothing supports 'roughly half'; we don't even know how big the gap in plea rates was.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: Last season, each of the five starting players on the Harbor City basketball team was named to the regional all-star squad, an honor reserved for the region's best individual players. No other team in the region had more than two all-stars. So Harbor City must have been the best team in the region last season.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the sportswriter's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the judgment of all-star selectors, who may know little about how well the players work together
presumes that a team made up of individually outstanding players must itself be outstanding as a team
takes for granted that the players were chosen for the all-star squad solely on the basis of their scoring
draws a conclusion about the team's performance in every season from evidence about a single season
takes for granted that the regional all-star squad included at least one player from every team in the region
questions.explanation: The sportswriter moves from the excellence of each starter to the excellence of the team as a whole, though a team of strong individuals can still play poorly together; B describes this. A is tempting because it mentions teamwork, but the argument's problem is not reliance on the selectors, whose judgment of individuals may be sound. The conclusion concerns only last season (D), and nothing presumes the players were chosen for scoring (C) or that every team had an all-star (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Harbor City was the best team in the region last season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All five of its starters were all-stars, an honor for the best individual players; no other team had more than two.

breakdown.analysis: So every starter was great. Does that make the team great? Five stars who won't pass the ball can lose to a team of role players. This is the part-to-whole flaw: what's true of each part isn't automatically true of the whole. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the argument moves from the players to the team.

choices.note: Tempting, since it hints at teamwork. But the argument doesn't lean on the selectors' view of teamwork; it treats their picks as evidence about individuals, which is fair. The jump comes after that, from individuals to team.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The selectors called him the best guard, and they don't even watch practice, so he must be the best guard.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each part outstanding, so the whole is outstanding. That's exactly the leap from five all-stars to the best team.
Nothing in the argument depends on why the players were picked. Any basis for the honor leaves the same gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: She led the league in points, so she must be the league's best defender too.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about last season. No other season is mentioned.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The team won the title this year, so it will be the best team every year.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need this. Even if some teams had no all-stars, the gap from players to team remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our school had the most students on the honor list, so every school must have sent someone.

questions.stimulus: Health official: The rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma in Tarrow County is twice the rate in neighboring Ellis County. Tarrow's air contains far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's air does, mostly from the freight yards that ring Tarrow's largest town. Therefore, reducing the amount of diesel exhaust in Tarrow's air would lower Tarrow's rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the health official's argument?
choices: Diesel exhaust is the primary cause of childhood asthma among the children who live in Tarrow County.
Ellis County has no freight yards or any other major source of diesel exhaust within its borders.
Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow County would also lower the rate of respiratory illness among adults living there.
Children with asthma attacks are likelier to be taken to a hospital in Tarrow County than in Ellis County.
Exposure to diesel exhaust can contribute to making some children's asthma severe enough to require hospitalization.
questions.explanation: If diesel exhaust could not worsen children's asthma to the point of hospitalization, cutting it would do nothing to the hospitalization rate, so the argument requires E. A is the tempting trap but is too strong: exhaust need only be one contributing factor, not the primary cause of asthma. B is not needed (Ellis need only have less exhaust), C concerns adults, and D would weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow would lower its childhood-asthma hospitalization rate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tarrow's rate is twice Ellis's; Tarrow's air has far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's.

breakdown.analysis: Two counties differ in exhaust and in asthma hospitalizations. So cutting exhaust will cut hospitalizations? Only if exhaust has something to do with kids ending up in the hospital. We need the minimal link: exhaust can play some part in making asthma severe enough to hospitalize.

choices.note: Too strong. Exhaust can matter without being the primary cause. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Diesel exhaust is not the primary cause of childhood asthma in Tarrow County.

choices.note: Too strong. Ellis just needs less exhaust than Tarrow, which the stimulus already says. Negating this changes nothing.
choices.negation: Ellis County has at least one freight yard or other major source of diesel exhaust.

choices.note: Adults are out of scope. Negate it and the argument about children is untouched.
choices.negation: Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow would not lower the rate of respiratory illness among adults there.

choices.note: Wrong direction. If Tarrow kids are just more likely to be hospitalized for the same attacks, that's an alternative explanation, which hurts the argument. And its negation doesn't hurt the argument either.
choices.negation: Children with asthma attacks are not more likely to be taken to a hospital in Tarrow than in Ellis.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: exhaust can't contribute to severe, hospital-level asthma in any child. Then reducing exhaust can't lower hospitalizations, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Exposure to diesel exhaust cannot contribute to making any child's asthma severe enough to require hospitalization.

questions.stimulus: Any field planted with winter rye after the harvest will lose less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would. After this fall's harvest, every one of the fields on the Hollis farm will be planted with winter rye, as the farm's owners have already arranged. It follows that the Hollis farm will qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only farms that plant winter rye on all of their fields after the harvest qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Every farm that qualifies for the county's soil-conservation grant loses less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would have.
Most farms that plant winter rye after the fall harvest qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant in that year.
Any farm all of whose fields will lose less soil to winter erosion than they otherwise would qualifies for the grant.
Winter rye reduces the amount of soil lost to winter erosion more than any other cover crop planted after the harvest does.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every Hollis field will lose less soil over the winter; D makes exactly that a sufficient condition for the grant, so the conclusion follows. A is the attractive trap, but 'only' gives a necessary condition for qualifying, not a guarantee. B reverses the needed conditional, C's 'most' cannot guarantee this farm qualifies, and E compares crops.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Hollis farm will qualify for the soil-conservation grant.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rye after harvest → field loses less soil over winter; every Hollis field will get rye.

breakdown.analysis: Chain the premises: every Hollis field gets rye → every Hollis field loses less soil. The conclusion jumps to the grant, which appears nowhere in the premises. We need a bridge from the premise-only idea (all fields lose less soil) to the conclusion-only idea (qualifies for the grant): all fields lose less soil → qualifies.

choices.note: Tempting, because Hollis plants rye on every field. But 'only' makes rye a requirement for the grant, not a ticket to it. Meeting a requirement doesn't guarantee qualifying.
This reverses the bridge: qualifies → loses less soil. We need loses less soil → qualifies.
Too weak. 'Most' leaves room for Hollis to be one of the farms that doesn't qualify.
CORRECT. Hollis fields all lose less soil, and this says any such farm qualifies. Conclusion guaranteed.
A comparison of crops. Rye being the best erosion fighter says nothing about the grant.

questions.stimulus: After farmers in the Kell Valley switched from flooding their orchards to drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to each tree's roots, they used about 30 percent less water per acre. Yet in the years after drip irrigation became widespread in the valley, the total amount of water drawn from the valley's aquifer for agriculture rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why agricultural water use in the Kell Valley rose?
choices: Drip irrigation made orchards profitable on hilly land that could not be flooded, so irrigated acreage expanded greatly.
Drip irrigation systems are considerably more expensive to install than the flood irrigation systems they replaced in the valley.
A few farmers in the valley continued to flood their orchards even after drip irrigation had become widespread there.
The amount of water drawn from the Kell Valley aquifer by households in the valley also rose during those years.
Drip irrigation sharply reduces the amount of water that is lost to evaporation before it reaches the trees' roots.
questions.explanation: Less water per acre can still mean more water in total if many more acres are irrigated; A supplies that increase in acreage. C is tempting, but holdouts who kept flooding would only limit the savings, not produce a rise above earlier levels. D concerns household rather than agricultural use, E explains only the per-acre savings, and B makes expansion less likely.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Drip irrigation cut water use per acre by about 30 percent, but total agricultural water use rose.

breakdown.analysis: Per acre went down, total went up. How? Total = per acre × number of acres. If the acres grew enough, the total can rise even while each acre uses less. Watch the switch from a rate to a total. We need an answer that grows the number of irrigated acres.

choices.note: CORRECT. More acres, each using less. If acreage grew by more than enough to offset the 30 percent savings, the total rises.
Higher cost would tend to slow adoption and expansion. It doesn't explain more total water use.
Tempting. Holdouts would make the savings smaller, but they were flooding before too. They can't push total use above where it started.
Households aren't agriculture. The puzzle is about water drawn for farming.
This explains the per-acre savings, one side of the puzzle. It does nothing to explain the rise.

questions.stimulus: Dr. Imani: Some residents want the city to stop fluoridating its water because a few people have reported mild tooth discoloration. But by that standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water, since chlorine sometimes gives water an unpleasant taste. No one seriously proposes ending chlorination, which protects against waterborne disease. So mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in Dr. Imani's argument by the claim that the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the claims about chlorine's taste and benefits are offered to support.
It is a premise offered in support of the residents' view that the city should stop fluoridating its water.
It is presented as an implication of the residents' standard, one that the argument treats as clearly unacceptable.
It is a claim that the argument concedes is true but maintains is irrelevant to the issue of fluoridation.
It is a subsidiary conclusion that is offered as the argument's only evidence that fluoridation causes no harm.
questions.explanation: Dr. Imani does not believe the city should stop chlorinating; she shows that the residents' standard (a minor side effect justifies ending a treatment) would require it, and since no one accepts that result, the standard fails. C describes this. A is wrong because the conclusion is the last sentence; B gets the direction backward; D and E misdescribe a claim the argument relies on and never offers as evidence of safety.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By the residents' standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating (chlorine sometimes tastes bad); no one seriously proposes ending chlorination.

breakdown.analysis: Does Dr. Imani think the city should stop chlorinating? No. That's the point. She takes the residents' rule (a minor side effect is enough to drop a treatment), applies it to chlorine, and gets a result everyone rejects. The author doesn't believe this claim. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. We need an answer that says it's a consequence of the residents' standard that the argument rejects.

choices.note: The main conclusion is the last sentence, about discoloration not being a good reason. The chlorine claim supports that, not the other way around.
Backwards. The claim is used against the residents' view, not for it.
CORRECT. It's what the residents' standard would commit the city to, and the next sentence shows nobody accepts it. That's how the standard gets rejected.

Tempting, because Dr. Imani does think the 'by that standard' link holds. But she doesn't call it irrelevant; it's the heart of her argument, and she certainly doesn't accept that chlorination should end.
Wrong role and wrong job. The claim isn't supported by other premises, and the argument never tries to show fluoridation causes no harm at all.

questions.stimulus: Five years ago, bottom trawling was banned throughout Selby Bay, ending a practice that had long torn up the seafloor where cod lay their eggs. Since the ban took effect, the number of juvenile cod counted in the bay's annual survey, which samples the same twenty sites each year, has tripled. Evidently, the ban has allowed the bay's cod population to recover.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Does bottom trawling also harm the populations of fish species other than cod that live in Selby Bay?
Did juvenile cod counts rise as much over the same period in nearby waters where trawling continued?
Was the ban on bottom trawling supported by most of the commercial fishing crews that work in Selby Bay?
Has the cost of enforcing the trawling ban in Selby Bay exceeded the estimates made before it took effect?
Was bottom trawling banned in Selby Bay before it was banned in the region's other bays?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the ban with the rise in juvenile cod, but a regionwide trend could explain it. If counts rose just as much where trawling continued, the ban looks irrelevant; if not, the ban is better supported, so B matters. A and E are on topic but do not bear on whether the ban caused this rise, and C and D concern politics and cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The trawling ban has allowed Selby Bay's cod population to recover.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Trawling (which tore up cod spawning grounds) was banned five years ago; since then juvenile cod counts have tripled.

breakdown.analysis: Cod came back after the ban. Was it the ban? Maybe cod came back everywhere: cooler water, fewer predators, a good spawning run. We need a two-sided question about a comparison group: what happened where nothing was banned? One answer helps the argument; the other hurts it.

choices.note: Other species are out of scope. The argument is about cod and whether the ban caused their rise.
CORRECT. Same rise next door where trawling continued? Then the ban probably didn't do it. Much smaller rise there? The ban looks like the cause. Either answer matters.
Fishers' opinions don't tell us whether the ban worked. Popularity isn't evidence.
Cost matters for policy, but not for whether the ban caused the cod to recover.
Tempting, since it's about other bays. But the order of the bans doesn't tell us whether cod rose there too, which is what we'd need.

questions.stimulus: Over the past season, the Elm Street Community Garden surveyed everyone who attended its Sunday composting workshops, asking whether the garden should ban chemical fertilizers on all of its plots. Eighty-five percent of the respondents said yes. Since the workshops are open to all of the garden's plot holders, the garden can conclude that most of its plot holders favor such a ban.
questions.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that plot holders who favor a ban would be willing to pay higher plot fees for organic alternatives
overlooks the possibility that a ban might attract new gardeners who have never attended a composting workshop
presumes, without providing justification, that the garden could enforce a ban on chemical fertilizers without hiring additional staff
infers that most plot holders favor a ban merely from the fact that a few plot holders have requested one
treats the views of plot holders who chose to attend composting workshops as representative of plot holders generally
questions.explanation: Being open to all plot holders does not make the workshop-goers a fair sample: people who choose to spend Sundays learning to compost are likely to be especially committed to organic methods, and so especially likely to favor a fertilizer ban. E describes this. D is tempting because it mentions a small group, but the survey covered every attendee and 85 percent agreed, not 'a few.' The argument says nothing about fees (A), recruiting (B), or enforcement (C).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the garden's plot holders favor banning chemical fertilizers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85 percent of the people who attended Sunday composting workshops said yes; the workshops are open to all plot holders.

breakdown.analysis: Open to everyone isn't the same as attended by a cross-section of everyone. Who gives up a Sunday to learn composting? Mostly gardeners already committed to organic methods, and they're exactly the people who'd want chemical fertilizers banned. It's like polling the members of a vegetarian cooking class about whether the cafeteria should drop meat. This is the unrepresentative-sample flaw. We need an answer that says the workshop-goers may not speak for all plot holders.

choices.note: The conclusion is about what plot holders favor, not what they'd pay for. Irrelevant.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Gardeners want a new shed, so they'll gladly pay double plot fees for one.

choices.note: So? Attracting new gardeners is a separate effect. The argument is about what current plot holders favor.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our current members like the rule, so we can ignore how it would affect future members.

choices.note: Enforcement is a practical issue the argument never touches. Its conclusion is only about plot holders' views.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Members favor a ban, so the garden can enforce it with the volunteers it already has.

choices.note: Tempting, since the flaw is about who was asked. But the garden asked everyone at the workshops and got 85 percent agreement, not a handful of requests. The problem is which plot holders were asked, not how few.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Two gardeners asked for a rain barrel, so most gardeners want one.

choices.note: CORRECT. The workshop-goers chose to attend, and they're likely the most organic-minded gardeners. Being 'open to all' doesn't make them typical of all plot holders.

questions.stimulus: City engineer: At the intersections where we replaced four-way stop signs with small traffic circles two years ago, collisions fell by 40 percent the following year. Drivers must slow down to get through a traffic circle, and slower speeds mean fewer collisions. So we should install traffic circles at all of the city's remaining four-way-stop intersections as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city engineer's argument?
choices: The intersections that were converted were chosen at random from among all of the city's four-way-stop intersections.
Many drivers report that they find traffic circles confusing the first few times they drive through them.
In the year before the conversion, the converted intersections had more collisions than any others in the city.
Traffic circles generally cost the city less to maintain each year than the traffic signals at other intersections do.
Some of the collisions that occurred at the converted intersections in the following year involved pedestrians or cyclists.
questions.explanation: The engineer generalizes from the converted intersections to the rest. If those intersections were picked at random (A), they are representative of the remaining ones, and a fluke at specially chosen sites is less likely to explain the drop. C is the trap: it actually weakens the argument, because intersections chosen for an unusually bad year would tend to improve anyway and may differ from the rest. D compares circles with signals, which is not the alternative under discussion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should install traffic circles at all remaining four-way-stop intersections.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Collisions fell 40 percent at the converted intersections the next year; circles force drivers to slow down, and slower speeds mean fewer collisions.

breakdown.analysis: So it worked at those intersections. Will it work at the others? Only if the converted ones were like the rest. If the city picked its worst intersections, a drop the next year might just be a bad year returning to normal. We need an answer that makes the converted intersections a fair test of the others.

choices.note: CORRECT. Random selection means the converted intersections are a fair sample of the rest, and it rules out the 'worst ones bounced back' explanation.
Confusion would, if anything, hurt the case. And it's about drivers' feelings, not collisions.

Tempting, because it shows the problem was real. But if these were the worst intersections, an unusually bad year could have simply returned to normal, and they may differ from the rest. That weakens the argument.
Wrong comparison. The choice is circles versus four-way stops, not circles versus signals. And cost isn't safety.
Who was in the remaining collisions doesn't tell us whether circles caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: Music teacher: Students who practice an instrument in many short sessions each week generally improve faster than students who practice for the same total amount of time in a few long sessions. Yet most of my students practice in a few long sessions each week, because they find those easier to fit into busy schedules of school, sports, and part-time jobs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the music teacher's statements?
choices: Students who practice in only a few long sessions each week do not improve in their playing at all.
Most of the music teacher's students improve more slowly than do the students of most other music teachers.
A student's schedule is the most important factor in how quickly that student's playing improves.
Some of the teacher's students would probably improve faster by spreading the same practice time over more sessions.
The music teacher should require students to practice in short sessions even if doing so is hard to schedule.
questions.explanation: Short sessions generally produce faster improvement for the same total time, and most of the teacher's students use long sessions, so some of them would probably improve faster by switching; D is appropriately hedged. A is too strong, since long sessions only produce slower improvement. E recommends a policy the statements never address, B compares students with other teachers' students, and C is an unsupported ranking.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. For the same total time, many short sessions generally beat a few long ones; 2. most of the teacher's students use a few long sessions, for scheduling reasons.

breakdown.analysis: Put the facts together: short sessions generally work better, and most of these students don't use them. So at least some of them are probably leaving improvement on the table. Watch for answers that exaggerate ('not at all', 'most important') or turn the facts into advice.

choices.note: Too strong. 'Improve faster' with short sessions means long sessions are slower, not useless.
Other teachers' students are never mentioned. We can't make that comparison.
Unsupported superlative. Schedules explain why students choose long sessions; nothing ranks schedule against other factors.
CORRECT. Same total time, more sessions: the first fact says that generally works better, and most of these students aren't doing it. 'Some' and 'probably' keep it safe.
Tempting, because it seems like the obvious lesson. But it's a recommendation, and the statements only describe. They never weigh scheduling burdens against improvement.

questions.stimulus: Coffee shops in Brayton that offer free wireless internet have, on average, higher daily revenue than Brayton coffee shops that do not, according to a recent survey of local businesses. A business consultant has therefore advised the owner of the Corner Cup, a Brayton coffee shop that does not offer wireless internet, that the shop would increase its daily revenue by offering it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultant's reasoning?
choices: Offering free wireless internet costs a coffee shop relatively little each month compared with its other expenses.
Most Brayton shops that offer wireless had higher revenue than other Brayton shops even before they began offering it.
Several of the Corner Cup's regular customers have asked its owner to begin offering free wireless internet.
Coffee shops in nearby towns that offer free wireless internet also tend to have higher daily revenue than those that do not.
Some Brayton coffee shops that offer free wireless internet have lower daily revenue than the Corner Cup currently does.
questions.explanation: The consultant infers from a correlation that wireless internet raises revenue. B shows the revenue gap existed before the service was offered, suggesting that busier shops tend to adopt wireless rather than wireless making shops busier. E is the trap: a comparison of averages allows some wireless shops to earn less, so E does nothing to undercut the claim. C and D tend to support the argument, and A concerns cost, not revenue.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Offering wireless internet would increase the Corner Cup's daily revenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brayton shops with free wireless have higher average daily revenue than those without.

breakdown.analysis: Shops with wireless earn more. Did the wireless do that? Maybe busy, well-funded shops are just the ones that add extras. The arrow could run the other way. We need an answer that shows the revenue gap doesn't come from the wireless.

choices.note: Cost isn't revenue. Cheap or not, the question is whether wireless brings in more money.
CORRECT. The wireless shops were already ahead before they had wireless. So the gap can't be credited to the wireless; success probably came first.
Customer requests make it a bit more likely that wireless would help. If anything, a strengthener.
More of the same correlation. It supports the consultant, if anything.
Tempting, because it shows some wireless shops doing worse. But the claim was about averages, and averages allow exceptions. This doesn't touch the causal question.

questions.stimulus: Prosecutors should offer a defendant a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea only if the defendant has no prior conviction for a violent offense. Moreover, in any case with an identifiable victim, such an offer should be made only after the victim has been informed of it.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Ortiz has no prior convictions of any kind, and the victim of his theft has been told of the proposed offer. So the prosecutor should offer Ortiz a reduced charge.
Pryce has a prior conviction for fraud, which is not a violent offense. So the prosecutor should not offer Pryce a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
Hale has no prior convictions, and the owner of the shop he vandalized has heard nothing about any plea offer. So it would be premature to offer Hale a reduced charge.
Lam's offense had no identifiable victim, though Lam has a prior conviction for assault. So the prosecutor may offer Lam a reduced charge once the community has been consulted.
The victim of Reyes's burglary was told of the proposed offer and objected to it. So the prosecutor should not offer Reyes a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
questions.explanation: The principle gives only necessary conditions: no prior violent conviction and, where there is an identifiable victim, the victim told first. So it can justify only a conclusion that an offer should not be made, at least not yet, when a condition fails. In C the shop owner is an identifiable victim who has heard nothing about any offer, so making the offer now would be premature. A is the trap: Ortiz meets both conditions, but meeting necessary conditions does not show that the offer should be made. E gives the victim a veto the principle never grants, B treats fraud as if it were violent, and D ignores Lam's assault conviction.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Offer a reduced charge → no prior violent conviction; in a case with an identifiable victim, offer → victim informed first.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must conclude that an offer should not be made (or not yet), because one of these conditions fails.

breakdown.analysis: Both rules are "only if" rules, so they give necessary conditions. Contrapositive: violent prior OR (identifiable victim not yet told) → no offer (yet). The principle can never tell you to make an offer; it can only tell you not to. So the right answer must: 1. conclude against an offer, at least for now; 2. rest on a condition that really fails. Most students pick (A) because Ortiz checks every box. It fails because passing "only if" conditions just means the offer isn't ruled out; nothing says it should be made. Necessary isn't sufficient. Also watch (C)'s stand-in wording: a shop owner is an identifiable victim, and "premature" means "not yet."

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Ortiz meets both necessary conditions, so the principle doesn't forbid the offer. But it never says when an offer should be made. This treats necessary conditions as sufficient.
Fraud isn't violent, so the first condition is met and the principle gives no reason to refuse. Misapplied.

CORRECT. The shop owner is an identifiable victim and hasn't heard about any offer. The second rule allows an offer only after the victim is told, so making it now is premature. Condition fails → not yet.
Lam has a prior assault conviction, a violent offense. The first rule says no offer, consultation or not. This gets the principle backward.
The principle requires only that the victim be told, not that the victim agree. This victim was told, so no condition fails. An objection isn't a veto here.

questions.stimulus: Sea otters, absent from Calder Sound for decades, returned there twelve years ago. Otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. In the years since the otters' return, the kelp forests in the sound have more than doubled in area. Thus, the otters' return is probably the main reason that the kelp forests have expanded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Sea otters eat more of Calder Sound's sea urchins than does any other predator that lives in the sound.
Nothing other than the otters' return has affected the kelp forests in Calder Sound during the past twelve years.
Expanded kelp forests provide the sea otters of Calder Sound with shelter from the predators that hunt them.
Before the otters returned, grazing by sea urchins was among the factors that kept the sound's kelp forests from spreading further.
The sea urchins in Calder Sound eat no food other than kelp, and nothing but otters ever preys on them.
questions.explanation: The argument's mechanism is otters → fewer urchins → more kelp. That works only if urchins were actually holding the kelp back before the otters came. Negate D and urchin grazing never limited the kelp, so removing urchins could not explain the expansion. B is the trap: it rules out every other influence, which sounds like the standard alternative-cause assumption, but the conclusion says only that the otters were probably the main reason, so other factors could have played some part. A and E are also stronger than needed, and C runs the relationship backward.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The otters' return is probably the main reason the kelp forests expanded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Otters returned twelve years ago; otters eat urchins and urchins eat kelp; since then kelp area has more than doubled.

breakdown.analysis: The chain is otters → fewer urchins → more kelp. Every link has to hold. What if urchins were never holding the kelp back? Then eating some of them changes nothing, and the otters can't be the reason. We need an answer that says urchin grazing was actually limiting the kelp before. Most students pick (B) because "rule out other causes" is the reflex for any causal argument. It fails because the conclusion only says "main reason." Other things can have nudged the kelp too. Negate (B) and the argument is still standing. A necessary assumption has to be needed, not just helpful.

choices.note: Too strong. Otters don't need to be the top urchin predator, just to cut urchin numbers enough to matter. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Some other predator in the sound eats at least as many urchins as the otters do.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It looks like the usual "no other cause" assumption. But the conclusion is only that otters were the main reason. Something else, like a small temperature shift, could have helped a little. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Something other than the otters' return has affected the kelp forests in Calder Sound during the past twelve years.

choices.note: This runs the wrong way: kelp helping otters, not otters helping kelp. Negating it doesn't touch the argument.
choices.negation: Expanded kelp forests do not provide the otters with shelter from their predators.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: urchin grazing wasn't limiting the kelp at all. Then fewer urchins can't explain more kelp, and the otter explanation collapses.
choices.negation: Before the otters returned, grazing by sea urchins was not among the factors keeping the kelp forests from spreading further.

choices.note: Way too strong. Urchins can eat other things and have other predators, and otters can still be the main reason. Negating it is harmless.
choices.negation: Sea urchins in Calder Sound eat some food other than kelp, or something besides otters preys on them.

questions.stimulus: Under the Ridgefield Swim Club's rules, any swimmer who breaks a club record during the season earns an invitation to the regional training camp. Odile, who swims for Ridgefield, received an invitation to this year's camp, and she trained harder this season than ever before. So Odile must have broken a club record this season.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every chef who completes the Marlow Institute's program learns to make stock from scratch. Petra never completed that program, even though she enrolled in it. So Petra must not know how to make stock from scratch.
Every apartment in the Elgin Building comes with a private balcony. Dev's apartment, which he has rented for six years, has no private balcony. So Dev's apartment must not be in the Elgin Building.
Yusuf must have spent over $100 on his last visit to Fenwick's, since he left the store with a discount coupon, and Fenwick's gives one to every customer who spends over $100 in a single visit.

Only applicants who pass the entrance exam are admitted to Carlow Academy. Lena, who studied for the exam all summer, was admitted to Carlow Academy this fall. So Lena must have passed the entrance exam.

Most volunteers who attend the orientation session stay with the literacy program for a full year. Malik attended this spring's orientation session. So Malik will probably stay with the program for a full year.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a sufficient condition as necessary: breaking a record guarantees an invitation, but an invitation could come for other reasons. C makes the same move, inferring big spending from the coupon, though it states its conclusion first and has no filler detail. D is the trap: it copies the original's order and even its irrelevant detail about hard work, but 'only' makes passing the exam necessary for admission, so its conclusion follows. A negates the condition instead of reversing it, B is a valid contrapositive, and E is a reasonable probabilistic inference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Odile must have broken a club record.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Breaks a record → invited; Odile was invited (and trained hard).

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X → Y; this one has Y; so this one must have X (affirming the consequent). The training detail is filler.

breakdown.analysis: Breaks a record → invited. Odile was invited. So she broke a record? Not necessarily: there may be other ways to earn an invitation, like a coach's pick or a fast time at a meet. The training detail is filler. We need the same move: X → Y; Y; so X. Most students pick (D) because it looks like a carbon copy, right down to the hard-work filler. But "only applicants who pass are admitted" means admitted → passed. Lena was admitted, so she passed. That's valid, so it can't match a flawed argument. Read "only" carefully: it marks the necessary condition. The right answer, (C), hides by leading with its conclusion; rearrange it and it's the same skeleton.

choices.note: A different error: X → Y; not X; so not Y (denying the antecedent). Petra could have learned to make stock somewhere else.
Valid. Every Elgin apartment has a balcony; Dev's doesn't; so it isn't in the Elgin Building. That's a correct contrapositive.
CORRECT. Rearranged: spends over $100 → coupon; Yusuf got a coupon; so he spent over $100. Same reversal. Coupons might also go out for birthdays or promotions.

Tempting, and the main trap. Same order, same filler. But "only applicants who pass are admitted" makes passing necessary for admission, so admission proves passing. Valid, so it doesn't share the original's flaw.
A modest "probably" drawn from a "most" premise. That's reasonable, not the same flaw.

questions.stimulus: Public health director: Of the Fallon County residents who were treated for heat stroke last summer, 70 percent were over the age of 65, and the share was similar the summer before. Clearly, then, the county's residents who are over 65 are much more likely to suffer heat stroke than are its younger residents, and our summer outreach should focus on them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the public health director's reasoning?
choices: It presumes, without providing justification, that heat stroke is more dangerous for older residents than for younger ones.
It treats a factor that makes heat stroke more likely as though it were the only possible cause of heat stroke.
It confuses the claim that most heat stroke patients are over 65 with the claim that most residents over 65 suffer heat stroke.
It fails to consider how the number of the county's residents who are over 65 compares with the number who are younger.
It overlooks the possibility that some of the younger residents treated for heat stroke also had other illnesses.
questions.explanation: That 70 percent of heat stroke patients were over 65 shows greater risk only if residents over 65 make up well under 70 percent of the population; if most residents are over 65, the figure is unremarkable. D points to that missing comparison of group sizes. C is the trap: it names a real and familiar confusion, but the director never concludes that most older residents get heat stroke, only that they are more likely to than younger residents. Nothing in the argument concerns danger (A), a sole cause (B), or other illnesses (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Residents over 65 are much more likely to suffer heat stroke than younger residents (so outreach should focus on them).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of last summer's heat stroke patients were over 65; the share was similar the summer before.

breakdown.analysis: So what if 70 percent of patients were older? What if 80 percent of the county is over 65? Then older people would actually be under-represented among patients. A share of patients means nothing without the share of the population. It's like saying most car crashes happen under 50 mph, so slow driving is dangerous: most driving is under 50. We need an answer that points at the population base rate. Most students pick (C) because they recognize the classic flip of "most A are B" into "most B are A." It fails because the director never says most older residents get heat stroke; the conclusion is comparative. The right answer hides in plain words: "how the number ... compares" is the base rate.

choices.note: The argument is about how likely heat stroke is, not how dangerous it is. Wrong dimension.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Older residents should get first priority for treatment, since heat stroke is surely more harmful to them.

choices.note: The director never says age is the only cause; "more likely" leaves room for other causes.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smokers get lung disease more often, so smoking must be the only cause of lung disease.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Mixing up "most patients are old" with "most old people are patients" is a real flaw, but this argument doesn't make it. The director's conclusion is comparative: older residents are more likely to get heat stroke than younger ones. No claim about most older residents.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most lottery winners buy tickets every week, so most people who buy tickets every week win the lottery.

choices.note: CORRECT. The patient share shows higher risk only if older residents are a smaller share of the population. If the county is mostly over 65, a 70 percent patient share is no surprise. Comparing the two groups' sizes is the base rate.
Other illnesses among younger patients don't affect the age comparison. If anything they'd make younger residents look riskier, not safer.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ten runners collapsed in the heat, so the heat caused every collapse, though several runners had heart conditions.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: A court ruling deserves public confidence only if it is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow. But a ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists cannot be explained in such terms unless the court sets out the specialists' competing views in plain language. In the Marsh case, the appellate court did not set out in plain language the views of either side's forensic experts. So the Marsh ruling does not deserve public confidence.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the legal scholar's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any court ruling that sets out specialists' competing views in plain language is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow.
A court ruling that is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow deserves the confidence of the public.
Most court rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists fail to set out the specialists' views in plain language.
The forensic experts in the Marsh case disagreed with one another about matters that ordinary citizens could not easily follow.
What the appellate court decided in the Marsh case depended on which side's forensic experts had the better of their dispute.
questions.explanation: The second rule applies only to a ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists. E says, in other words, that the Marsh ruling did: the outcome depended on which side's forensic experts were right. Then, since the experts' views were not set out plainly, the ruling was not explained in followable terms, and by the first rule it does not deserve confidence. D is the trap: it shows the experts disagreed, but not that the ruling turned on their dispute, so the second rule is never triggered. A and B reverse the stated conditionals, and C's 'most' says nothing about this case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Marsh ruling does not deserve public confidence.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Deserves confidence → explained in followable terms; for a ruling that turns on a specialist dispute, followable → specialists' views set out plainly; the Marsh court did not set out either side's forensic experts' views plainly.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Rule 2, contrapositive: turns on a specialist dispute AND views not set out plainly → not followable. Rule 1, contrapositive: not followable → no confidence. Marsh: views not set out plainly. What's missing? Whether the Marsh ruling turned on a dispute among specialists at all. Without that, rule 2 never kicks in. Full chain: Marsh turned on expert dispute + views not set out → not followable → no confidence. Most students pick (D) because it puts the experts in a dispute about hard matters, which feels like the missing piece. It fails because experts disagreeing isn't the ruling turning on their disagreement; the court could have decided on other grounds. (E) hides behind a paraphrase: "depended on which side's experts had the better of their dispute" means "turned on a dispute among specialists."

choices.note: Reverses rule 2. Setting out the views plainly is necessary for a followable explanation; this makes it sufficient. It's also about rulings that DO set them out, and Marsh didn't.
Reverses rule 1. Being followable is necessary for confidence, not sufficient. And it only tells us about followable rulings, while we're trying to show Marsh isn't one.
"Most" rulings tells us nothing about Marsh. A sufficient assumption has to lock in this case.

Tempting, and the main trap. There's a dispute in the case, but rule 2 needs the RULING to turn on it. The court might have decided Marsh on a procedural point. Then rule 2 doesn't apply and the conclusion doesn't follow.
CORRECT. If the decision depended on which experts were right, the ruling turned on a specialist dispute. Rule 2 plus the unexplained views → not followable; rule 1 → no public confidence.

questions.stimulus: Most commuters in Pell City choose between driving downtown and taking the train mainly on the basis of total travel time. The city plans to add express trains that would cut the train trip downtown by ten minutes. But it also plans to close two of the three parking lots at the Maple Street station, where most train commuters board after driving there. Unless they can quickly park elsewhere, the time saved may be lost searching for a space. So ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the city should cancel its plan to close two of the three parking lots at the Maple Street station
the express trains may not, by themselves, make the train more attractive to commuters than it is now
the number of commuters who take the train downtown will decline once the two parking lots are closed
commuters care more about the availability of parking near the station than about their total travel time
most commuters who now drive downtown would switch to the train if parking at the station were expanded
questions.explanation: Commuters weigh total travel time, and the ten minutes saved on the train may be lost hunting for parking, so the express trains may fail to make the train more attractive; B matches the argument's cautious 'may.' C is the tempting trap but is too strong: the argument says only that the savings may be lost, not that ridership will fall. A draws a policy recommendation the argument does not reach, D contradicts the first sentence, and E goes beyond the facts.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Commuters choose mainly on total travel time; 2. express trains would save ten minutes on the train; 3. two of three lots at the main boarding station will close; 4. unless commuters park quickly elsewhere, the saved time may be lost to parking.

breakdown.analysis: The argument is building toward a cautious point: the time gain from express trains might be eaten by the parking hunt. So the express trains may not help the train win commuters. Watch for answers that go further than 'may': predicting a decline, or telling the city what to do.

choices.note: Adds a recommendation. The argument points out a problem; it never weighs whether the lots should stay open.

CORRECT. Ten minutes saved, maybe ten minutes lost parking. If total time doesn't improve, and total time is what commuters care about, the express trains may not make the train any more attractive. The 'may' matches the stimulus.
Tempting, because closing lots sounds bad for ridership. But 'will decline' is too strong. The time saved and lost might simply cancel out.
Contradicts the first sentence: commuters choose mainly on total travel time. Parking matters only as part of that time.
We don't know this. Nothing says how many drivers would switch under any plan.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: The Halvorsen Museum should not lend its fragile, one-of-a-kind medieval tapestry to the touring exhibition, even though the tour would let many thousands of people see the tapestry who otherwise never would. Each move exposes the tapestry to a small but real risk of irreparable damage, and once it is damaged, no future visitor will ever see it as it is now.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the museum director's argument?
choices: A museum should lend its works only to exhibitions organized by institutions with a recognized expertise in the conservation of fragile textiles.
Museums should make the works in their collections accessible to as many members of the public as they reasonably can.
A museum should not lend a work if conditions in the galleries of the borrowing institution could damage the work.
The risk of damage to a work should be weighed against the benefit of showing it to new audiences.
Wider viewing now never justifies even a small risk that later viewers can no longer see a work as it is.
questions.explanation: The director concedes the tour's benefit, wider viewing, but holds that a small risk of irreparable damage outweighs it, since damage would mean no later visitor could see the tapestry as it now is. E states that trade-off as a rule about later viewers, which is exactly the director's reason. D is the trap: it describes weighing risk against benefit, which the director does, but it does not say which way the balance comes out, so it cannot justify refusing the loan. C concerns the borrower's galleries, while the director worries about the moves; A turns on facts the stimulus never gives; and B supports lending.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The museum should not lend the tapestry to the touring exhibition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The tour would let many thousands more people see it (concession); each move carries a small but real risk of irreparable damage; once damaged, no future visitor will see it as it is now.
