breakdown.analysis: Why should a small risk beat thousands of viewers? The director's answer is the future: damage is forever, and every later visitor loses out. We need a principle that says that kind of risk outweighs wider viewing now. Most students pick (D) because "weigh risk against benefit" sounds like exactly what the director did. It fails because a weighing rule doesn't say which side wins; you could weigh and decide to lend. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The right answer talks about "later viewers" instead of the tapestry, so it can look off-topic at first.

choices.note: The stimulus says nothing about who organized the tour or their textile expertise. We can't apply this.
Opposite. This supports lending.
The director's worry is the moves themselves, not the borrower's galleries. Wrong source of risk.
Tempting, and the main trap. The director does weigh risk against benefit. But this principle doesn't say which way the scale tips, so it can't get you to "don't lend."
CORRECT. The tour lets more people see the tapestry now; each move risks damage that would keep later viewers from ever seeing it as it is. The principle says that's never worth it, so don't lend.

questions.stimulus: Most of the orchards in the Daltry region that were sprayed with kaolin clay last season suffered little sunburn damage to their fruit. Every orchard in the region that suffered little sunburn damage got a premium price for its apples. So some of the orchards in the region that were sprayed with kaolin clay got a premium price for their apples.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the musicians in the Fairview orchestra studied at a conservatory. Most musicians who studied at a conservatory can sight-read difficult scores. So some musicians in the Fairview orchestra can sight-read difficult scores.

Every bicycle sold at Corliss Cycles comes with a one-year warranty. Most bicycles that come with a one-year warranty are made overseas. So some of the bicycles sold at Corliss Cycles are made overseas.

Most of the novels on this year's prize shortlist were written by first-time authors. Some first-time authors have received writing grants. So some novels on the shortlist were written by authors who received writing grants.

Some restaurants that passed last month's health inspection got a reminder notice from the city. After all, most restaurants that passed were also inspected the year before, and every restaurant inspected the year before got one.

Every greenhouse at the Ames nursery is heated entirely by solar panels. No greenhouse that is heated entirely by solar panels needs a backup generator. So none of the greenhouses at the Ames nursery needs a backup generator.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B is C, so some A are C. D has exactly this form once it is rearranged: it gives its conclusion first, then 'most that passed were inspected the year before' and 'every restaurant inspected the year before got a notice.' A is the trap: it matches the original's order and also concludes 'some,' but its second premise says 'most' rather than 'every,' and two 'most' statements need not overlap, so it is invalid. B and C are likewise invalid, and E is valid but has a different, all-and-none form.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some orchards sprayed with kaolin clay got a premium price.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most sprayed orchards had little sunburn damage; every orchard with little sunburn damage got a premium price.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; all B are C; so some A are C (valid).

breakdown.analysis: Is it valid? Yes. The A's that are B (most of them) are all C, because every B is C, so at least some A's are C. We need another valid "most + every → some" argument. Most students pick (A) because it reads in the same order and ends with the same "some." But its second link is "most," not "every." Two "mosts" can miss each other: the orchestra's conservatory graduates could be the ones who can't sight-read. The right answer, (D), states its conclusion first and its premises after "After all." Rearrange before you match.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Same order, same "some" conclusion. But "most" in the second premise breaks it: the orchestra's conservatory graduates could all be in the minority who can't sight-read. Invalid, so not parallel to a valid argument.
Every A is B; most B are C; so some A are C. Invalid: the Corliss bikes could all be among the warranty bikes made at home.
"Some first-time authors" got grants, but they need not be the shortlisted ones. Invalid.
CORRECT. Rearranged: most that passed were inspected the year before; every one inspected the year before got a notice; so some that passed got a notice. Most A are B, all B are C, so some A are C.
Valid, but a different shape: all A are B, no B is C, so no A is C. No "most," no "some."
